APPENDIX G
Capital Facilities Financial Plan

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
The Capital Facility Financial Plan (CFFP) presents a plan for financing capital facilities identified
in Clark County’s 20-year Comprehensive Growth Management Plan (2025-2045), as required by
Washington State’s Growth Management Act (GMA). It covers the following types of capital
facilities: transportation; parks and open space; stormwater drainage and water quality; and
county buildings and other facilities. The plan covers the 6-year period from 2026-2031.

The plan provides for:

    •   Expenditures totaling $1.116 billion over the 6-year period.
    •   Appropriated resources, such as grants, user fees, voter-approved bonds and legally
        dedicated revenues, to finance over 70% (or $1.046 billion) of the expenditure program.
    •   General purpose funding sources --To complete the financing of its overall capital facilities
        program, Clark County has the option to allocate additional funds from its general-
        purpose resources.
    •   Revenues from new development – Clark County is anticipating receiving $70.4 million
        from new development sources.
    •   Stormwater facilities for present and future developments are paid for by project
        developers, not the county.

The following Table G.1 summarizes the expenditures and resources included in this plan:

Like any long-term plan, the financing plan laid out in this document depends upon a number of
forecasts and assumptions about future conditions. As time passes, it is expected that this plan will
be modified and updated to reflect changing circumstances and financial realities. Year-by-year
implementation of the plan will be carried out within the County’s budgeting process and other
appropriate processes.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE
Washington State’s Growth Management Act (GMA) sets forth the requirements for local growth
management plans in RCW 36.70A.070 (3). One of the requirements is for a capital facilities plan,
which must include at least a 6-year financial plan for funding future capital facilities within
projected funding capacities, which identifies the sources of public funds. The capital facilities plan
for Clark County encompasses chapter 6 of the Comprehensive Growth Management Plan
(CGMP), along with relevant portions of other supporting documentation. This document is
intended to identify funding sources for the principal capital facilities provided by Clark County
itself. Financing for facilities provided by entities other than Clark County, such as the cities within
the county, school districts and fire districts can be found in the CGMP.

Since the CFFP is strictly financial in nature, it does not directly address capital facilities
constructed by the private sector and subsequently donated to the county. Examples of such
facilities include local streets constructed within subdivisions, local sewer hook-ups and on-site
stormwater detention/infiltration facilities serving new developments. Such facilities are
indirectly addressed in that their existence mitigates the need for impact fees or System
Development Charges (SDC) to construct them.

This document is also restricted to capital costs. It does not attempt to address issues relating to
the need for the on-going maintenance and operation of capital facilities. These issues will be
addressed in Clark County’s annual budgeting process. Since this document focuses on the 6-year
time frame required by the Growth Management Act, specifically the years from 2023-2028, long-

  Stormwater facilities for present and future developments are paid for by project developers, not the
county.

range 20-year projections of expenditures and resources are available elsewhere for most types
of facilities. The CFFP is chiefly intended to demonstrate the overall financial feasibility of Clark
County’s 6-year capital facilities plan, so it does not contain detailed, project-level information.

This document is not intended to provide a year-by-year spending plan or cash flow analysis. Nor
does it address the specific structure or timing of bond issues, where new debt is called for. These
details should be developed during the county’s annual budgeting process or through other
appropriate processes. The information presented in this document is based on data provided by
county staff in both oral and written form. Finally, this document represents a long-range plan and,
thus, may be revised as appropriate to reflect changing financial conditions and the changing needs
of the community.

EXPENDITURES AND APPROPRIATED RESOURCES
The following pages show the planned expenditure levels for each type of capital facility along
with funding sources that are earmarked for each facility type. For example, the Transportation
section shows planned expenditures for road construction, along with road-related grants and
traffic impact fee revenues, which may be used to finance those expenditures. For some facility
types, the appropriated revenues are sufficient to finance the entire expenditure program. In
other cases, general-purpose resources are needed to supplement the appropriated revenues.
(Sources of general-purpose funding are discussed in the following section.)

Some of the appropriated revenue sources already exist. Examples include road fund property
taxes, transportation and park impact fees and the proceeds of the conservation futures bond
issue. Other sources, such as certain grants, have not yet been received, but are expected without
the need for major action on the part of the County Council. Finally, certain appropriated sources
described in this section will not materialize without specific action by the Council and are
identified in the following pages.

Expenditures outlined in this section are divided into those related to “existing needs” and those
resulting from “new development.” This categorization is approximate and is based upon
information included in the Comprehensive Growth Management Plan. The basis for
categorization is identified for each facility type. Revenue sources are similarly classified for each
facility type.

EXISTING NEEDS AND NEW DEVELOPMENT
Clark County has in place a system of transportation impact fees based on analysis of the road
service levels and the impact of new development on the transportation network. On this basis,
project costs totaling $151.6 million are allocated to “New Development.” These costs are
financed with a mix of traffic impact fees and other sources of public funds. The remainder of the
construction program, totaling $99 million, reflects existing transportation needs. The public and
private share of growth-related projects are included in the “New Development” Column of this
table. The public share reflects the portion of the project that is allocable to current demand, while
the private share is the portion that is allocable to future growth. Revenues in the “New
Development” column include impact fees, which are used to fund a project’s private share, as well
as other public funding sources that support these projects.

EXISTING NEEDS AND NEW DEVELOPMENT:
The National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) Phase I Municipal Stormwater
Permit (Permit) requires the county to have a Stormwater Management for Existing Development
(SMED) program to prevent or reduce impacts to waters of the state caused by discharges from
the municipal separate storm sewer system (MS4). The SMED aligns with WAC 365-196-415(3)(c)
in that it includes major maintenance and rehabilitation of the existing stormwater system and
addresses stormwater management deficiencies in already developed areas.

Under the Permit, the SMED program must consider projects including new flow control facilities,
new water quality treatment facilities, new Low Impact Development (LID) management
practices, retrofits of existing facilities, repairs costing more than $25,000, and property
acquisition to provide water quality or flow control benefits. The program may also consider other
projects to address impacts, including restoration of riparian buffers or forest cover, floodplain
reconnection, permanent removal of impervious surfaces, street sweeping, line cleaning, and
watershed collaboration.

The Six-year Stormwater Capital Plan is updated annually and implemented by the Clean Water
Division to meet the SMED requirements.

The Stormwater Capital Plan is funded primarily through the Clean Water Fee charged to owners
of property in unincorporated areas of Clark County. Other significant funding sources are
competitive grants and Real Estate Excise Tax II (REET II) dollars.

The Stormwater Capital Plan does not provide capacity for new development; rather, it facilitates
improvements to the existing stormwater system to enhance water quality performance as
required by the Permit. For this reason, projects in the Stormwater Capital Plan are exclusively
considered under the ‘Existing Needs’ category.

Stormwater infrastructure associated with new development is paid for by the developer, and is
required to meet standards for stormwater treatment and flow control in the Clark County
Stormwater Manual.

GENERAL PURPOSE RESOURCES
In prior capital facilities plans, available resources included the Real Estate Excise Tax (REET) to
pay for capital improvements of County buildings and facilities. Available resources include the
existing .25% REET(1) and an additional 0.25% REET(2) authorized by the Growth Management Act
specifically to finance capital projects. Together, both of these resources are committed to
existing capital needs over the period covered by this capital facilities plan. REET is a tax on the sale
of real property and can be volatile depending on economic and market conditions.

REET 1 Fund revenues can be used mainly for planning, acquisition, construction, reconstruction,
repair, replacement, rehabilitation, or improvement of streets, roads, highways, sidewalks, streets,
and road lighting systems, traffic signals, bridges, domestic water systems, storm and sanitary
sewer systems, parks, recreational facilities, law enforcement facilities, fire protection facilities,
trails, libraries, administrative facilities, judicial facilities, river flood control projects, waterway
flood control projects in some jurisdictions, housing projects in some jurisdictions, technology
infrastructure that is integral to a capital project.

Recent changes to REET I include:

The use of REET 1 to fund the maintenance of, operation of, and service support for existing
capital projects (that meet the definition of capital project), including services to residents of
affordable housing or shelter units under RCW 82.46.015 is revised with HB 1791. Most recently,
the use of REET 1 for maintenance of capital projects was limited to $100,000 or 25% of available

A PPENDIX G                                                                                          228
                                       CLARK2045
funds, with a cap of $1,000,000 per year. This threshold has been changed to $100,000 or 35% of
available funds, with no cap.

REET 2 Fund revenues can be used mainly for public works projects of a local government for
planning, acquisition, construction, reconstruction, repair, replacement, rehabilitation, or
improvement of streets, roads, highways, sidewalks, street and road lighting systems, traffic
signals, bridges, domestic water systems, storm and sanitary sewer systems, and planning,
construction, reconstruction, repair, rehabilitation, or improvement of parks.

Recent Changes to REET II include:

New language added to RCW 82.46.035 (pursuant to adoption of HB 1791) stating that REET 2
revenues may also be used for “any use allowed under RCW 82.46.010 [REET 1]."

Under RCW 82.46.035(5)(c), local governments were allowed (until January 1, 2026), to use REET
2 funds for the: planning, acquisition, construction, reconstruction, repair, replacement,
rehabilitation, or improvement of facilities for those experiencing homelessness and affordable
housing projects.

The threshold for use of REET II funds was $100,000 or 25% of available funds for those capital
projects, not to exceed $1,000,000. Under HB 1791, the expiration date and the $1,000,000 cap
have been removed. Additionally, a new section has been added to RCW 82.46.035 that allows
REET 2 funds to be used towards projects supported through an interlocal housing collaboration
as established under chapter 39.34 RCW, such as affordable housing projects or facilities for
individuals experiencing homelessness.

Amendments have also been made to RCW 82.46.037. This includes an increase to 35% of
available REET 2 funds and removal of the $1,000,000 cap for “the operation of, the maintenance
of, and service support for, existing capital projects as included in the definition of capital project
in RCW 82.46.035(4) and RCW 82.46.010(6)(b),” subject to meeting existing requirements.
Additionally, reporting requirements once found in RCW 82.46.037 have been eliminated.

The language requiring REET 2 funds be “deposited in a separate account after December 31,
2023” has also been eliminated.

FUND BALANCE
Fund balance represents surpluses that have been accumulated by the county in past years. Best
viewed as “non-renewable resources,” fund balances are available to finance major one-time
expenditures. Appropriate expenditures might include County buildings and facilities. Fund
balance is probably less appropriate as a funding source for parks acquisition and development
because the expenditures included in this 6-year plan are just a portion of the total 20-year parks
program. An ongoing source of funds, such as the REET (see above) is needed to support the parks
program.

Available fund balances needed to complete the financing of the capital facilities plan are shown in

POLICY IMPLICATIONS
This section recaps the Council actions necessary to implement this financial plan, outlines the
overall, long-term financial impact of this plan on the county and highlights the role of the budget
process in implementing, monitoring and modifying this plan.


IMPLEMENTATION ACTION NEEDED
As discussed above, a number of Council actions are needed to implement this financial plan. These
include:

    •    Implementing a funding mechanism for any identified funding gaps for the
         capital facilities program.
   •    Implementing a funding mechanism (such as a property tax or tipping fee) sufficient to
        generate enough funds for the Conservation Areas Acquisition Program.
    •   Ensure that the rates charged by the county to its wholesale customers are adequate
        to repay bonds issued for expansions. Maintaining a sewer rate structure adequate to
        cover the costs of future expansion.
    •   Approval of the Capital Planning Advisory Committee (CPAC) capital improvement plan
        (CIP) each year during the Annual Budget Process.
    •   Implementing a funding mechanism sufficient to generate enough funds for
        the Capital Planning Program.


LONG-TERM FINANCIAL IMPACT
Implementation of this financial plan will have an impact on the county’s financial condition
extending well beyond the six-year time horizon of the plan itself. While it is difficult to foresee the

231                                                                                      A PPENDIX G
                                      CLARK2045
implications of these effects, it is important to be aware of them. The following points should be
kept in mind:

   •    Most or all of the revenue from the existing Conservation Futures property tax
        levy will be committed to servicing bonds re-issued in 2018 for the next twenty
        years. Thus, a significant source of funding for the parks program contained in this
        plan will not be available again until 2038.
   •    Revenues from the Real Estate Excise Tax (REET) are committed to servicing debt
        on the Public Service Center and Community Health Center (first and second
        issue). Revenues from the REET may be available to meet this need, depending
        upon economic and market conditions and other community needs.
   •    A portion of the Fund balance accumulated in recent years has been expended. This
        may limit the county’s ability to meet unanticipated needs in future years.

BUDGET PROCESS IMPLICATIONS
This document is a long-term plan. Responsibility for the year-to-year financial decisions needed
to implement the plan will fall to the county’s budget process. Key tasks the budget process will
need to perform include the following:

   •    Monitoring economic conditions and revenue estimates and, when necessary, modifying
        the financial plan to address changing conditions.
   •    Monitoring project expenditures to ensure that they remain within planned levels and,
        when necessary, modifying the financial plan to address changing conditions.
   •    Deciding the timing of the expenditures and debt issuance within the six-year time frame of
        the financial plan.
   •    Managing operating expenditure levels to ensure adequate funding for the maintenance of
        capital facilities developed under this plan.
   •    Reviewing the needs and priorities of the community and, when necessary, modifying the
        capital plan and its financial elements accordingly.


IMPACT ON HOUSEHOLDS
In some areas, this financial plan calls for new fees or taxes. The following summarizes the
estimated financial impact of the changes described on individual households. These are estimates
only and, in certain cases, the decisions needed to precisely quantify the impacts have not yet
been made.

    •   Transportation: No new taxes or fees anticipated within the 6-year time frame as outlined
        in this document.
    •   Parks and Open Space: A funding strategy will be needed to enable the Conservation
        Areas Acquisition Program. Originally contemplated using the Conservation REET,
        funding options also includes a property tax and garbage tipping fees, among others.



A PPENDIX G                                                                                     232
                                    CLARK2045
  •   County Buildings and Other Facilities: A funding strategy will be necessary to pay for
      the capital and major maintenance cost and some of the future funding may need to
      come from voter approved bonds or tax increases.

 14.1.1       The county and the cities of Battle Ground, Camas,          Climate       GHG
              Ridgefield, Vancouver, and Washougal shall cooperate
              to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, reduce vehicle
              miles traveled per capita, and improve environmental
              justice through development of a greenhouse gas
              emissions reduction subelement in each local
              government’s respective comprehensive plan, and its
              related development regulations that identify the
              actions the jurisdiction will take during the planning
              cycle that will:

              a) Result in reductions in overall greenhouse gas
              emissions generated by transportation and land use
              within the jurisdiction but without increasing
              greenhouse gas emissions elsewhere in the state or
              region;
              b) Result in reductions in per capita vehicle miles
              traveled within the jurisdiction but without increasing
              greenhouse gas emissions elsewhere in the state or
              region; and
              c) Prioritize reductions that benefit overburdened
              communities in order to maximize the cobenefits of
              reduced air pollution and environmental justice.

              Greenhouse gas reduction subelements shall be
              consistent with Chapter 36.70A, Department of
              Commerce guidelines, and supported by scientifically
              credible projections and scenarios. [GHG]
 14.1.2       Greenhouse gas reduction subelements shall be               Climate       GHG
              developed with an overall target of reaching net-zero
              greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 in alignment with
              the statewide greenhouse gas emissions reductions set
              forth in RCW 70A.45.020(1) and in accordance with all
              applicable laws. Individual jurisdictions may choose to
              set greenhouse gas reduction targets more ambitious
              than the statewide goals. Jurisdictions shall use a
              consistent methodology for measuring greenhouse gas
              emissions reduction progress over time using each
              jurisdiction’s individual 2022 (or 2023 inventory for the
              City of Vancouver) greenhouse gas emissions inventory
              for baseline greenhouse gas emissions values and
              establishment of the scientifically credible inventory
              protocol to use moving forward to track progress.
              [GHG]

 14.1.7       The county and each municipality shall cooperate to           Climate       RES
              equitably enhance resiliency to, and avoid or
              substantially reduce the adverse impacts of, climate
              change in human communities and ecological systems
              through goals, policies, and programs consistent with
              the best available science and scientifically credible
              climate projections and impact scenarios that moderate
              or avoid harm, enhance the resiliency of natural and
              human systems, and enhance beneficial opportunities
              through development of a resiliency subelement in
              each local government’s respective comprehensive
              plan, consistent with Chapter 36.70A.

              Specific goals, policies, and programs of the resiliency
              subelement must include, but are not limited to, those
              designed to:

              a) Identify, protect, and enhance natural areas and
              green infrastructure to foster resiliency to climate
              impacts, as well as areas of vital habitat for safe passage
              and species migration;
              b) Identify, protect, and enhance community resiliency
              to climate change impacts, including social, economic,
              and built environment factors, that support adaptation
              to climate impacts consistent with environmental
              justice; and
              c) Address natural hazards created or aggravated by
              climate change, including landslides, flooding, drought,
              heat, smoke, wildfire, and other effects of changes to
              temperature and precipitation patterns.

              Each jurisdiction’s resiliency subelement must prioritize
              actions that benefit overburdened communities that
              will disproportionately suffer from compounding
              environmental impacts and will be most impacted by
              natural hazards due to climate change. [RES]

 14.2.1       Implement Climate Element policies in alignment with          Climate   GHG; RES
              following guiding principles:
              a) Evaluate who is most impacted by the issue or
              decision (positively or negatively), what the data tells us
              (consider qualitative and quantitative data), and what
              ways the recommended action could be modified to
              enhance positive impacts or reduce negative impacts.
              b) Prioritize engagement with communities vulnerable
              and at risk from climate impacts.
              c) Design engagement to align with the unique
              characteristics of vulnerable populations that are at
              higher risk from climate impacts.
              d) Directly limit harm, address past harm where
              possible, and be effective at reducing greenhouse gas
              emissions and/or improving resilience.
              e) Collaborate with communities and community
              organizations and consult with Tribes (and seek funding
              necessary to support collaboration). Community
              organizations include, but are not limited to: local non-
              governmental organizations and businesses, service
              providers, faith based institutions, and partner
              government agencies.
              f) Design projects to help communities meet their day-
              to-day needs and build resilience in the face of climate
              impacts. Climate actions should avoid creating harm to
              vulnerable populations by, for example, compounding
              day-to-day financial burdens or making climate impacts
              worse.
              g) Remove barriers to participation and to benefits.
              Make climate projects, programs, and their associated
              benefits, easily accessible. Barriers to participation
              include physical and non-physical barriers. Examples
              include: access and safety challenges for people with
              certain physical health conditions or developmental
              disabilities, language barriers, financial assistance
              program requirements, availability of food, childcare,
              and transportation, and meeting time or location
              convenience.
              h) Provide culturally inclusive outreach and educational
              information in multiple languages and formats with
              accurate translations.
              i) Design educational opportunities for multiple
              audiences and ages and seek opportunities to integrate
              county efforts with community initiatives (i.e. cultural
              arts, youth, community organization, or school
              programs).
              j) Help create a healthier environment and community.
              [GHG, RES]

14.3.6    Develop resilience hubs — community-serving facilities       Climate       RES

          reduce carbon pollution while enhancing quality of life.

          a) Resilience hubs (or hubs) can be regularly open

 14.17        Promote a just approach to increasing clean, renewable,   Climate       GHG; RES
              and diverse building energy options in unincorporated
              Clark County to achieve net zero greenhouse gas
              emissions. [GHG, RES]
 14.17.1      Implementation of policies under this goal shall:         Climate       GHG; RES
              consider various scales of projects (utility-scale,
              community-scale, and household scale), prioritize
              benefits for people who rent housing or commercial
              space and households and businesses with limited
              income, avoid causing harm in overburdened
              communities, and involve community education and
              feedback. [GHG, RES]
 14.17.2      Promote self-reliance and community capacity to           Climate       RES
              respond to emergencies, such as with distributed
              energy resources and energy management systems,
              microgrids, and virtual power plants. [RES]
 14.17.3      Pursue innovations to expand and improve accessibility    Climate       GHG
              to a diversity of clean renewable energy options.
              Renewable energy resources are defined in RCW
              54.04.190. Clean renewable energy includes renewable
              resources that have low or zero greenhouse gas
              emissions.

              Examples include but are not limited to:
              a) Collaborate with Northwest Natural and Clark Public
              Utilities on utility-led decarbonization plans and
              renewable energy programs
              b) Remove barriers for renewable energy in site and
              building design
              c) Facilitate efficient siting of renewable energy
              development
              d) Facilitate the development of community-owned,
              small-scale renewable energy generation projects
              e) Advance pilot projects to test emerging and heritage
              technologies and collect community feedback on
              projects to inform next steps
              f) Facilitate learning opportunities from projects in
              other communities [GHG]

 14.23        Effectively implement Climate Element policies [GHG,         Climate       GHG; RES
              RES]
 14.23.1      Develop and maintain county government staff                 Climate       GHG; RES
              members' capacity, technical expertise, and skills
              related to climate change and environmental justice so
              as to improve countywide policy implementation,
              equity, and resilience. [GHG, RES]
 14.23.2      Establish a clear and coordinated approach for               Climate       GHG; RES
              organizing implementation of Climate Element policies
              across county departments, including a designated
              department for leading implementation coordination
              and designated staff across departments to lead
              implementation of specific policies. [GHG, RES]
 14.23.3      Develop Climate Element priority policies and                Climate       GHG; RES
              greenhouse gas emissions inventory updates in
              alignment with the mandatory 5-year Department of
              Commerce Climate Element monitoring and reporting
              schedule. For each 5-year cycle, identify
              implementation successes and barriers to progress to
              help inform priorities for the next 5-years. [GHG, RES]
 14.23.4      Reduce unincorporated Clark County greenhouse gas            Climate       GHG
              emissions and county operations emissions to net-zero
              by the year 2040 with incremental targets as follows,
              where percent reductions are based on a 2022
              baseline:
              a) 80% reduction by 2030;
              b) 87.5% reduction by 2035; and,
              c) 95% reduction by 2040 [GHG]
 14.23.5      Provide the County Council an annual work session on         Climate       GHG; RES

              should include progress toward our greenhouse gas
              reduction targets; significant actions completed during
              the previous year; measurable emissions reductions
              where available; costs and savings where available;
              significant barriers encountered; and opportunities to
              improve progress in the coming year. (See policies
              14.14.2 and 14.14.3 for specific fleet reporting metrics.)

RESOURCE DOCUMENT 3: EQUITY AND
ENVIRONMENTAL JUSTICE LENS
This resource document is a copy of the Equity and Environmental Justice Lens completed on June 18,
2024 as part of the Climate Element development process.


INTRODUCTION
With the passage of E2SHB 1181 during the 2023 Washington state legislative session, Clark
County is now required to add a Climate Change Element to its Comprehensive Plan by December
31, 2025.

The legislation emphasizes that planning and policy decisions related to climate change do not
impact us all in the same way. To this end, it requires policies in the Climate Change Element to,
“avoid creating or worsening localized climate impacts to vulnerable populations and
overburdened communities.” It also states that jurisdictions should encourage the participation of
vulnerable populations and overburdened communities in processes to develop and adopt
comprehensive plans. Furthermore, land use goals and policies, “must give special consideration to
achieving [environmental justice], […] including efforts to avoid creating or worsening
environmental health disparities.” RCW 36.70A


LOCALIZED CONTEXT
As a supplement to ES2HB 1181, the Washington State Department of Commerce provided
guidance to jurisdictions for incorporating the consideration of environmental justice and equity
into the Climate Change Element. This guidance acknowledged the importance of local
jurisdictions developing their own tools of analysis that are reflective of local context, informed by
local expertise, and are created with consideration for the social, cultural, political, and geographic
realities of their jurisdiction.

The guidance laid out some criteria to inform jurisdictional approach and some key questions
specific to equity:

   •   Co-governance: Does the measure show potential to build self-determination for frontline
       communities of color and/or low-income communities?

   •   Targeted Universalism: Is the measure clear on rights to healthy communities, and explicit
       in targeting interventions to communities furthest from achieving those rights?

   •   Accountability: Does the measure show potential to directly limit harm and hold those
       responsible accountable? Does it prioritize effectiveness?




A PPENDIX I                                                                                       304
                                        CLARK2045
    •   Community Wealth Building: Does the measure show potential to invest in and sustain
        local livelihoods, starting with communities with the greatest barriers to meeting their
        needs, through sustainable resource use and cooperative work?

Working from the legislation and Commerce guidance, Clark County developed this Equity and
Environmental Justice Lens with input and guidance from the Environmental Justice Coalition
(EJC) and began by focusing on specific high-level prompts centered on people, place, and process.
The EJC includes 15 community-based organizations and is one of three advisory groups
supporting the county’s Climate Project. The categories for analysis provided below form the
foundation for the Equity and Environmental Justice Lens for Clark County’s Climate Change
Element:

    •   People: Questions that focus on vulnerability and risk (from climate impacts), and the
        unique characteristics of populations that contribute to risk. Understanding what creates
        risk or vulnerability is critical to developing policies that mitigate negative impacts and
        more equitably distribute benefits.

    •   Place: These questions consider disproportionate burden from place-based environmental
        risk or vulnerability, and the relationships of populations with geographies and the natural
        and built environment. Understanding the connection between where people live and the
        distribution of hazards, or protective factors, is important to mitigate risk and elevate
        benefit.

    •   Process: Questions that ensure that goals and policies are informed by community input
        and relevant data sources.


EQUITY AND ENVIRONMENTAL JUSTICE LENS
The following questions can be utilized in multiple ways. As discussion prompts, analysis of policy
concepts, and as a mechanism to ensure that final goals and policies are mitigating negative impacts and
identifying strategies to ensure that most vulnerable and overburdened populations experience benefits
from the implementation of the Climate Element.

    •   Who is most impacted by this issue or decision? (positively or negatively)

        Understanding how different communities may or may not experience an issue is critical to
        ensuring that policies distribute benefits and burdens in an equitable way. In other words,
        Climate Element policies should not disproportionately impact populations who are
        overburdened, vulnerable, or who already experience health disparities. As you respond to this
        question, consider the physical, environmental, social, financial, cultural, mental health, and
        spiritual impacts of a policy.

        Additional prompts to support the analysis or discussion:




305                                                                                         A PPENDIX I
                                       CLARK2045
           o   Does this policy address barriers for specific communities to experience the benefits? If
               not, what will be done to address those barriers?

           o   Have we considered the historical or current relationship to the issue/policy for all
               communities?

           o   How does the policy seek to account for historical harm or create new opportunities for
               communities who are overburdened?

   •   What does the data tell us? (consider qualitative and quantitative data)

       Utilizing data (both quantitative and qualitative) is an important part of understanding impacts.
       These may be geographic, for example, looking at hazard risks across Clark County, or could
       reflect demographic data for how specific populations may be affected.

       As you use data to inform policy development, ensure you are intentional about the data that you
       use. Because of both the limitations and complexities of many data sets, it may be important to
       explore alternative data sets (for example, identifying community-generated data that can inform
       the policy decision). Ensure that you have also considered story and narrative that can provide
       additional contextual information, and that the policy is aligned with any community
       engagement input that has been provided.

       Additional prompts to support the analysis or discussion:

           o   How have community input and priorities been considered?

           o   What were the demographics of community engagement input? Are there critical voices
               or experiences that are not reflected in the engagement?

   •   What are the ways in which a policy recommendation could be modified to enhance
       positive impacts or reduce negative impacts?

       Policies developed through an Equity and Environmental Justice Lens should result in positive
       benefits across populations, while ensuring that there are targeted strategies to distribute
       benefits to overburdened, vulnerable, and communities that experience health disparities.

       Ensuring that policy language and impacts meet that vision may require specific modifications
       that can ensure positive benefit and mitigate or reduce negative effects.

       Additional prompts to support the analysis or discussion:

           o   Does this policy address barriers for specific communities to experience benefits? If not,
               what will be done to address those barriers?




A PPENDIX I                                                                                            306
                                       CLARK2045
           o   Does this policy build capacity for communities, or have the effect of increasing trust? Are
               there elements of the policy that can serve to heal communities who have experienced
               harm or experienced trauma from this issue/policy?


KEY DEFINITIONS
Below are definitions of key terms as defined by RCW 36.70A.030.

           •   "Overburdened community" means a geographic area where vulnerable
               populations face combined, multiple environmental harms and health impacts, and
               includes, but is not limited to, highly impacted communities as defined in RCW
               19.405.020.

           •   “Environmental justice" means the fair treatment and meaningful involvement of
               all people regardless of race, color, national origin, or income with respect to
               development, implementation, and enforcement of environmental laws,
               regulations, and policies. Environmental justice includes addressing
               disproportionate environmental and health impacts in all laws, rules, and policies
               with environmental impacts by prioritizing vulnerable populations and
               overburdened communities and the equitable distribution of resources and
               benefits.

           •   "Vulnerable populations" means population groups that are more likely to be at
               higher risk for poor health outcomes in response to environmental harms, due to:
               (i) Adverse socioeconomic factors, such as unemployment, high housing and
               transportation costs relative to income, limited access to nutritious food and
               adequate health care, linguistic isolation, and other factors that negatively affect
               health outcomes and increase vulnerability to the effects of environmental harms;
               and (ii) sensitivity factors, such as low birth weight and higher rates of
               hospitalization.

           o   "Vulnerable populations" includes, but is not limited to:

                      Racial or ethnic minorities;

                      Low-income populations; and

                      Populations disproportionately impacted by environmental harms.

TITLE VI NOTICE
Clark County hereby gives public notice that it is the County’s policy to assure full compliance
with Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, as amended, the Civil Rights Restoration Act of 1987,
and related statutes and regulations in all programs and activities. Title VI and related laws require
that no person shall on the grounds of race, color, sex or national origin be excluded from
participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be otherwise subjected to discrimination under any
Federal Aid Highway program or other activity for which Clark County receives Federal financial
assistance.

Any person who believes they have been aggrieved by an unlawful discriminatory practice under
Title VI has a right to file a formal complaint with Clark County. Any such complaint must be in
writing and with the Clark County Public Works Title VI Coordinator within one hundred, eighty
(180) days following the date of the alleged discriminatory occurrence. The Title VI Complaint
Procedures and Form may be obtained from the Title VI Coordinator at no cost to the complainant
by calling 564-397-2282 or visiting our Public Works Title VI the website at:
https://www.clark.wa.gov/public-works/title-vi-requirements-and-related-information.

origen nacional o sexo según lo dispuesto en el Title VI of the Civil Rights Act de 1964, según
enmendada, sea excluida por participar en, ser negado los beneficios de, o ser discriminado por
cualquier programa o actividad patrocinada por el condado. Para preguntas relacionadas con el
programa de Title VI de Obras Públicas del condado de Clark, o para servicios de interpretación

расы, цвета кожи, национальности или пола - как это предусмотренно Разделом VI Закона о
Гражданских Правах от 1964 года с поправками - не должен быть исключён из участия, или
получить отказ в выгодах, или в иной форме быть ущемлён в любой программе или
деятельности, спонсируемой Округом Кларк. По вопросам, связанным с Программой Раздела VI
департамента Общественных работ Округа Кларк, или по вопросам перевода для людей,
говорящих на ином языке кроме английского, или для получения материалов в альтернативном
формате, обращайтесь к координатору Раздела VI департамента Общественных работ Округа
Кларк по электронной почте CCPW-TitileVI@clark.wa.gov или по телефону 564.397.2282. Люди
с нарушениями слуха или речи могут обратиться в Вашингтонский центр переключения по

TIÊU ĐỀ VI/ĐẠO LUẬT NGƯỜI MỸ KHUYẾT TẬT

Chính sách của Hạt Clark là đảm bảo không ai bị loại trừ, bị từ chối quyền lợi hoặc bị phân biệt đối
xử trong bất kỳ chương trình hoặc hoạt động nào do hạt tài trợ dựa trên chủng tộc, màu da,
nguồn gốc quốc gia hoặc giới tính theo Tiêu Đề VI của Đạo Luật Dân Quyền năm 1964 sửa đổi.
Nếu quý vị có câu hỏi liên quan đến Chương Trình Tiêu Đề VI của Clark County Public Works
hoặc về dịch vụ thông dịch dành cho người không nói tiếng Anh hoặc về việc cung cấp tài liệu ở
định dạng thay thế, vui lòng liên hệ với Điều Phối Viên Tiêu Đề VI của Clark County Public Works
qua email CCPW-TitleVI@clark.wa.gov hoặc số điện thoại 564.397.2282. Người khiếm
thính/khiếm ngôn có thể gọi Washington Relay Center theo số 711.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
This Transportation ADA Transition Plan for Public Rights-of-Way (Plan) (ADA Transition Plan or
Plan) documents Clark County Public Works’ approach to achieving and maintaining accessibility
in the public pedestrian transportation network within Clark County’s jurisdiction. The Plan is
intended to meet the transition plan requirements applicable to public entities under Title II of the
Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) and its implementing regulations (28 CFR Part 35),
including 28 CFR § 35.150(d), and to integrate with Clark County’s ADA self-evaluation
obligations under 28 CFR § 35.105.

This Plan focuses on transportation infrastructure elements within public rights-of-way (PROW),
including sidewalks, curb ramps, pedestrian crossings and access routes, detectable warning
surfaces, pedestrian signal pushbuttons, accessible pedestrian signals (APS) where applicable, and
related barriers affecting accessible pedestrian travel.

Clark County has performed and continues to refine a pedestrian facility inventory and self-
evaluation of barriers in the public right-of-way, including the inventory work described in the
Clark County Right of Way Self-Evaluation Study. Inventory data is used to identify barriers,
assess severity, and support prioritization and programming of improvements.

The ADA Transition Plan targets county-owned facilities within the public road right-of-way in
unincorporated Clark County, such as sidewalks, curb ramps, pedestrian push buttons, and
driveway entrances. It excludes new active transportation facilities, which are covered by other
plans such as the County’s Six-Year Transportation Improvement Program (TIP) and
Comprehensive Plan. This Plan does not address buildings, privately owned facilities, or the
facilities owned by the incorporated cities and towns of Clark County.

KEY INVENTORY FINDINGS SUMMARY
Inventory findings summarized below are drawn from the Clark County Right of Way Self-
Evaluation Study (Clark County GIS Department, 2019) and are provided to characterize the
scope of barriers identified in the county-maintained public right-of-way pedestrian network in
unincorporated Clark County. The full, location-specific inventory is maintained in County records
and is used to support project scoping and prioritization.

Curb ramps: The Self-Evaluation Study reports a total of 10,073 curb ramp locations inventoried
in unincorporated Clark County. Of these, 6,735 locations (66.9%) were visually rated as fully

325                                                                                    A PPENDIX L
                                      CLARK2045
compliant or compliant except for missing detectable warning domes, and 1,147 locations (11.4%)
were identified as missing a curb ramp where one is required to serve a legal crossing.

Sidewalk conditions: The Self-Evaluation Study identifies multiple categories of sidewalk defects
and obstructions. Based on the categories with quantified values, the Study reports at least 8,190
defect observations, including cracking (4,109), spalling (2,069), and obstructions such as poles
and mailbox posts (973). The Study also notes driveway-related sidewalk conditions as an
inventory category with values identified as “Unknown,” indicating additional data development
may be needed for that category.

Missing sidewalks: The Self-Evaluation Study’s GIS analysis of the sidewalk layer identifies a total
of approximately 482.4 miles of missing urban sidewalks across roadway classifications in
unincorporated Clark County.

Pedestrian signals and APS: The Self-Evaluation Study reports that 101 pedestrian pushbutton
locations were measured and that 99 locations were ADA compliant (approximately 98%). The
Study further reports that 98% of the pedestrian pushbuttons evaluated have APS functionality.


P L A N N I N G -L E V E L C O S T E S T I M A T E S
The Clark County ADA Transition Plan provides a planning-level estimate of costs to address
identified ADA barriers in the public right-of-way pedestrian network. The cost analysis identifies
relevant components from the Pierce County ADA Transition Plan as well as cost data from
previous projects of similar scopes. Historical bid tabulations were reviewed and analyzed to
develop planning-level unit costs adjusted to 2026 dollars.

Curb ramps and sidewalks, costs are reflected by:

       Low impact improvements involve replacing facilities in kind with minimal grading or
       Reconfiguration requires no right-of-way acquisition and is relatively straightforward to
       implement.

       Mid-impact improvements include mitigation of obstructions, reconfigurations, some
       grading, and a moderate level of design effort, while still not requiring ROW acquisition.

       High-impact improvements require ROW acquisition and involve significant grading,
       extensive paving, substantial design efforts, as well as survey and utility coordination.

Rates and Inflation

A combined allowance of 30-50 percent was applied to construction costs to account for design,
permitting, inspection, and general construction administration. In addition, an annual inflation
rate of 5 percent was applied to escalate costs to 2026 dollars. This Plan treats cost estimates as
preliminary planning information subject to refinement through engineering scoping,
prioritization, and budget programming.

The preliminary total costs are based on linear feet (LF) to construct or rebuild curb ramps or
sidewalks. There are approximately 5,784 curb ramps with a mid-impact cost of $7,340 each. The
overall cost to complete all the curb ramps deficiencies is $42,454,560. The length of missing
sidewalk is 2,239,604 LF at a cost of $311 per LF. The overall cost of fixing all the missing
sidewalks would be $696,516,844.

Accessible Pedestrian Push Buttons

Low-impact improvements involve upgrading existing push buttons and controllers where the
current push button locations already meet ADA placement requirements. High-impact
improvements include relocating signal poles to compliant locations within the intersection, new
push button controllers and accessible push buttons. The APS unit costs reflect only the push
button equipment, controllers, and associated poles. Costs for curb ramps or sidewalk
modifications related to APS upgrades are not included.


IMPLEMENTATION APPROACH SUMMARY
Clark County Public Works implements accessibility improvements through a combination of
stand-alone ADA compliance projects, integration of ADA upgrades into road preservation and
capital improvement projects, and ongoing maintenance and repair activities. Consistent with
federal guidance, curb ramp upgrades are addressed as part of roadway alterations and
resurfacing activities where applicable. The County also uses inventory and public input to
prioritize locations for barrier removal.

INTRODUCTION AND PURPOSE
Clark County Public Works provides transportation facilities and services in the public right-of-
way that must be accessible to individuals with disabilities. Title II of the ADA prohibits

327                                                                                    A PPENDIX L
                                      CLARK2045
discrimination by public entities and requires that County programs, services, and activities be
accessible when viewed in their entirety. When structural changes to facilities are needed to
achieve program accessibility, public entities must develop and maintain a transition plan that
identifies barriers, describes methods to remove them, provides a schedule for action, and
identifies the official responsible for implementation (28 CFR § 35.150(d)).

This Plan is intended to serve as Clark County Public Works’ transportation-focused transition
plan for public rights-of-way. It is prepared to support County review, adoption, and public
availability as part of the County’s ongoing ADA compliance program. The transition plan lays out
how and when the county will upgrade pedestrian facilities to achieve compliance with the ADA
requirements. The self-evaluation report provided in Appendix A will be periodically updated as
planned improvements are completed.


PLAN AUDIENCE AND USE
This Plan is written for County decision-makers, Public Works staff, partner agencies, and
members of the public. It is designed to support practical implementation—inventory
management, project scoping, prioritization, funding, construction, and reporting.


HOW TO USE THIS PLAN
The Plan is organized to: (1) describe applicable legal requirements and County responsibilities;
(2) summarize the County’s self-evaluation and barrier inventory approach; (3) present findings
and barrier categories; (4) establish prioritization and implementation methods; (5) provide a
schedule framework and implementation tools; and (6) document public participation, grievance
procedures, and plan maintenance steps. Appendices include procedures, templates, and priority
list from the public survey.

ADA LEGAL FRAMEWORK
This Plan is grounded in federal civil rights requirements and accessibility design guidance
applicable to public entities and the public right-of-way. The primary authorities and guidance
include the following:

•   Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (Title II), 42 U.S.C. §§ 12131–12165.
•   Title II implementing regulations, 28 CFR Part 35, including § 35.105 (Self-Evaluation) and §
    35.150 (Program Accessibility; Transition Plans).
•   2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design (for elements within their scope).
•   Public Right-of-Way Accessibility Guidelines (PROWAG) issued by the U.S. Access Board as
    technical guidance for public rights-of-way accessibility; referenced by the County as an
    engineering and evaluation resource.
•   Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) accessibility-related provisions for
    pedestrian signals and pushbuttons, including accessible pedestrian signal (APS)
    considerations where applicable.

•     Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) and U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ)/U.S.
      Department of Transportation (DOT) technical assistance regarding curb ramps,
      resurfacing/alterations, and maintenance of accessible pedestrian routes.


REGULATORY REQUIREMENTS FOR TRANSITION PLANS
Under 28 CFR § 35.150(d), a public entity with 50 or more employees must develop a transition
plan when structural changes are necessary to achieve program accessibility. At a minimum, the
transition plan must: (1) identify physical obstacles that limit accessibility; (2) describe methods
that will be used to make facilities accessible; (3) specify a schedule for taking the steps necessary
to achieve compliance; and (4) indicate the official responsible for implementation.

This Plan is intended to satisfy these minimum elements for the transportation public right-of-way
scope addressed herein, in coordination with Countywide ADA transition planning activities.

RELATIONSHIP TO SECTION 504 AND OTHER
ACCESSIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 prohibits discrimination on the basis of disability in
programs and activities receiving federal financial assistance. Many transportation funding
programs involve federal assistance; therefore, Section 504 obligations may apply in addition to


329                                                                                             A PPENDIX L
                                      CLARK2045
the ADA. Clark County also maintains non-discrimination obligations under Title VI of the Civil
Rights Act of 1964 and related federal and state requirements.

This Plan is focused on ADA Title II transition planning for public rights-of-way transportation
infrastructure. It is intended to complement—not replace—other County non-discrimination and
accessibility policies and procedures.

SCOPE OF THE TRANSPORTATION ADA TRANSITION
PLAN

TRANSPORTATION FACILITIES COVERED
For purposes of this Plan, transportation facilities and infrastructure within the County’s public
rights-of-way may include, as applicable:

•   Sidewalks and pedestrian access routes, including continuous accessible routes to and through
    intersections.
•   Curb ramps and blended transitions at street crossings and other locations where pedestrian
    routes transition between sidewalk/landing areas and the roadway.
•   Detectable warning surfaces at curb ramps and other required locations.
•   Pedestrian crossing features such as marked crosswalks, curb returns, refuge islands, and
    accessible landing areas within Public Works’ transportation scope.
•   Pedestrian signal pushbuttons and APS features where signals are present and within County
    responsibility.
•   Maintenance-related barriers that impede accessible pedestrian travel (e.g., significant
    vertical displacement, obstructions, surface defects, vegetation encroachment) within Public
    Works’ control.


GEOGRAPHIC AND JURISDICTIONAL SCOPE
This Plan addresses transportation infrastructure within the Clark County public right-of-way
system for which Clark County Public Works has responsibility. In general, this includes facilities
within unincorporated Clark County and other locations where the County owns or maintains
transportation infrastructure. Facilities within city jurisdictions, state highways, or private
developments may involve separate responsible entities; this Plan does not assign responsibilities
to those entities unless supported by County source materials.


OUT OF SCOPE TOPICS
This Plan is limited to transportation-related public right-of-way infrastructure. Building interior
accessibility, parks accessibility, and other non-transportation facility programs are addressed
through other County ADA efforts and are outside the primary scope of this Plan. Where a



A PPENDIX L                                                                                      330
                                       CLARK2045
transportation barrier interfaces with a building entrance or public facility, coordination may be
required, but the public transportation right-of-way scope remains the focus.

CLARK COUNTY PUBLIC WORKS ADA
COMMITMENT
Clark County Public Works is committed to providing equitable access to County transportation
facilities and services for people with disabilities. The County’s objective is to create and maintain
an accessible pedestrian network that supports safe, independent travel, consistent with ADA
Title II program accessibility requirements.

Public Works use a combination of system inventory, prioritization, project programming, design
standards, construction practices, and maintenance activities to reduce and remove barriers over
time, subject to available funding and engineering feasibility considerations as allowed under
applicable law.

ADA COORDINATOR AND OFFICIAL RESPONSIBLE
FOR PLAN IMPLEMENTATION
Clark County designates an ADA Coordinator to coordinate Countywide ADA compliance efforts,
including grievance procedures and ADA program administration. For transportation public right-
of-way accessibility implementation, Clark County Public Works is the lead implementing
department for facilities within its transportation responsibilities, coordinated with the County
ADA Coordinator.

PUBLIC NOTICE, EFFECTIVE COMMUNICATION, AND
GRIEVANCE PROCEDURES
Clark County provides public notice regarding ADA rights and maintains procedures to ensure
effective communication with individuals with disabilities, consistent with 28 CFR Part 35. The
County’s grievance procedure provides a process for receiving and resolving ADA-related
complaints and requests for accommodation.

This Plan references the County’s established ADA grievance procedure and recommends that
Public Works maintain a transportation-specific intake and tracking process for public right-of-
way accessibility requests, coordinated with the County ADA Coordinator.

to Public Works transportation facilities.

SELF-EVALUATION BACKGROUND AND
METHODOLOGY
Clark County’s ADA self-evaluation for the public right-of-way provides the technical foundation
for this Transition Plan. The self-evaluation identifies barriers affecting accessible pedestrian
travel and methods used to inventory and assess facilities. The self-evaluation also informs
prioritization and implementation planning.


S E L F -E V A L U A T I O N A N D I N V E N T O R Y B A C K G R O U N D
The Clark County Right of Way Self-Evaluation Study describes inventory work that has been
conducted over multiple years. The Study notes that barriers have been identified since at least
2011 and that a comprehensive inventory of pedestrian facilities—including sidewalks, curb
ramps, and pedestrian signals—was developed using GIS-based data collection and analysis.

The Study further notes that, in 2019, the County provided an inventory using a curb ramp visual
inspection method (based on PROWAG 2011 and the 2010 ADA Standards) and that it assessed
sidewalk conditions and missing sidewalk locations using GIS layers. The Study describes
subsequent refinement of curb ramp measurement and evaluation methods using a more detailed
measurement form as needed for construction scoping.

INVENTORY METHODS BY FACILITY TYPE

CURB RAMPS
The Self-Evaluation Study describes curb ramp evaluation using a visual inspection rating system
(Ranks 1–6) and notes that curb ramps are further measured using a more detailed measurement
form for noncompliant features when construction scoping is required. The Study indicates that
the County transitioned from a 2015 curb ramp measurement form to the Washington State
Department of Transportation (WSDOT) ADA Curb Ramp Measurement Form (2018) for more
objective, measure-based evaluation in support of compliance determinations and design.

SIDEWALKS
Sidewalk inventory methods include identification of surface defects (e.g., cracking, spalling,
vertical displacement), obstructions, and missing sidewalk segments using GIS layers. The Study
describes a sidewalk inspection/scoring approach based on a scale that considers defect type and
severity.

PEDESTRIAN SIGNALS AND PUSHBUTTONS
Pedestrian signal and pushbutton inventory methods include measurement of installation and
operating features relevant to accessibility, including pushbutton reach range and height, and
identification of APS functionality where present. The Study reports a high rate of compliance for

TRANSPORTATION INFRASTRUCTURE ACCESSIBILITY
FINDINGS
This section summarizes the primary barrier categories identified in the County’s public right-of-
way pedestrian infrastructure inventory and self-evaluation. Findings are organized by facility
type and are intended to guide prioritization and corrective action planning.


CURB RAMPS
Curb ramp barriers include missing curb ramps at legal crossings, steep running or cross slopes,
improper alignment or landing geometry, inadequate width, excessive lips, and missing detectable
warning surfaces. The Self-Evaluation Study’s visual inspection results indicate that while many
curb ramps are compliant or near compliant, a substantial number require upgrades or
replacement, and over one thousand locations were identified as missing ramps where required.

Curb ramp compliance determinations and design solutions must consider applicable accessibility
criteria, construction constraints, and—where full compliance is not structurally feasible—
documentation of “maximum extent feasible” (MEF) outcomes consistent with federal
requirements for alterations.


SIDEWALKS AND PEDESTRIAN ACCESS ROUTES
Sidewalk barriers include vertical displacement, cracking, spalling, ponding, cross slope issues,
surface obstructions, vegetation encroachment, and missing segments that break route
continuity. Where sidewalks are missing, pedestrians may be forced into the roadway shoulder or
travel lanes, creating both accessibility and safety concerns.

A continuous accessible pedestrian access route requires not only adequate sidewalk presence,
but also compliant curb ramps, stable and slip-resistant surfaces, and avoidance of protruding
objects and obstructions within the pedestrian pathway.


P E D E S T R I A N S I G N A L S , P U S H B U T T O N S , A N D AP S
Accessible pedestrian signals and pushbutton accessibility may include pushbutton reach range
and mounting height, actuation force, locator tone and audible/tactile features where APS is used,
and alignment with the crossing direction. The Self-Evaluation Study reports that 99 of 101
measured pushbutton locations were ADA compliant (approximately 98%) and that 98% of
evaluated pushbuttons have APS functionality.

According to data from RTC and Clark County Public Works, there are 629 intersections on
county roads. The Self Evaluation Report notes that Clark County policy is to install APS at all

337                                                                                     A PPENDIX L
                                      CLARK2045
county intersections with traffic signals, and when pedestrian signals are altered, consistent with
best practice and applicable federal requirements for altered facilities.


CROSSING AND INTERSECTION ACCESSIBILITY
Intersection accessibility barriers may include missing or noncompliant curb ramps, inadequate
landing areas, insufficient crosswalk alignment, lack of detectable warnings, inadequate refuge
island features, and construction-related temporary route disruptions.

Where roadway preservation or capital projects affect intersections, Public Works should review
curb ramps and pedestrian access routes to ensure ADA compliance is addressed as part of the
project scope, including the obligation to provide curb ramps at altered crossings.

METHODS USED TO IMPROVE ACCESSIBILITY
Clark County Public Works uses multiple implementation mechanisms to remove or reduce
accessibility barriers in the public right-of-way. This section describes those methods at a program
level. Specific project lists, locations, schedules, and budgets must be confirmed through County
programming documents (e.g., Transportation Improvement Program) and project records.


A DA C O M P L I A N C E P R O J E C T S A N D AD A I M P R O V E M E N T
PROGRAM
Public Works implements stand-alone ADA compliance projects that focus on curb ramp
upgrades, detectable warnings, sidewalk connectivity, and pedestrian signal improvements. These
projects may be coordinated with the County’s annual road preservation program and may be
delivered in grouped locations to improve geographic efficiency.

The County’s Public Works ADA curb ramp improvement project webpage provides examples of
preservation and ADA improvement projects that include curb ramp construction and upgrades,
sidewalk connectivity enhancements, and pedestrian pushbutton modernization at multiple
locations.


INTEGRATION WITH ROAD PRESERVATION AND ALTERATION
PROJECTS
Federal guidance and ADA requirements generally require that curb ramps and accessible
pedestrian routes be addressed when a public entity alters streets, roads, or highways, including
certain resurfacing and reconstruction activities that affect pedestrian crossings. Public Works
will integrate curb ramps and pedestrian access route upgrades into roadway preservation and
capital improvement projects where pedestrian facilities are affected by the work.




A PPENDIX L                                                                                     338
                                     CLARK2045
Public Works should apply a consistent internal process to determine when a roadway project
triggers curb ramp upgrades at affected intersections and crossings, and to document decisions
when design constraints require MEF outcomes.


SIDEWALK MAINTENANCE, REPAIR, AND SPOT IMPROVEMENTS
Maintenance and repair activities can reduce barriers such as vertical displacement, surface
defects, and obstructions. Public Works may address sidewalk defects through maintenance
programs and spot improvements, prioritizing locations with high severity or high public use.
Maintenance activities should also address vegetation encroachment and debris that reduces the
clear width of accessible pedestrian routes.


TRAFFIC SIGNAL AND PUSHBUTTON UPGRADES
Traffic signal modernization projects provide opportunities to upgrade pedestrian pushbuttons
and APS features where required. Based on the Self-Evaluation Study, Clark County generally
installs APS when pedestrian signal systems are altered. Public Works will continue to integrate
accessibility upgrades into signal projects consistent with MUTCD requirements and applicable
ADA obligations.


DEVELOPMENT REVIEW AND PRIVATE DEVELOPMENT
COORDINATION
Development and redevelopment projects can create or improve pedestrian facilities in the public
right-of-way. Public Works and Community Development functions may coordinate to ensure
that required frontage improvements meet accessibility standards and that curb ramps and
sidewalks are constructed to applicable specifications.


CONSTRUCTION ACCESSIBILITY AND TEMPORARY PEDESTRIAN
ACCESS ROUTES
During construction and maintenance activities, temporary pedestrian access routes must be
provided when existing accessible routes are disrupted. Public Works will require contractors and
in-house crews to maintain accessible pedestrian access, including temporary route signage,
stable surfaces, and safe crossings consistent with applicable standards and best practices. Clark
County Public Works requires that county’s standard specifications and construction traffic
control requirements for maintaining accessible temporary pedestrian access routes (TPAR)
during construction and maintenance activities are adhered to.

PRIORITIZATION FRAMEWORK FOR ADA
IMPROVEMENTS
Because the County’s public right-of-way barrier inventory is extensive, implementation must be
prioritized to achieve meaningful accessibility improvements over time. Prioritization supports
the transition plan schedule required by 28 CFR § 35.150(d) and helps direct limited resources to
locations with the greatest access benefit and risk reduction.


PRIORITIZATION PRINCIPLES
Clark County Public Works will prioritize barrier removal using a combination of
condition/severity, functional importance, and equity considerations. Prioritization should remain
transparent, repeatable, and tied to measurable criteria where possible.

•   Severity of barrier and degree to which it limits access for people with disabilities (e.g., missing
    curb ramps, extreme slopes, blocked access route).
•   Connectivity and continuity of the pedestrian network, including routes to and between public
    facilities, community services, and key destinations.
•   Safety risk factors (e.g., pedestrians are forced into travel lanes due to missing sidewalks).
•   Public requests and documented access needs.
•   Coordination opportunities with planned roadway preservation, capital projects, or
    development work to improve efficiency and reduce rework.
•   Geographic equity and service to areas with higher concentrations of people with disabilities,
    when supported by reliable data.


CURB RAMP PRIORITIZATION APPROACH
The Self-Evaluation Study describes a curb ramp visual inspection ranking system (Ranks 1–6)
that provides a preliminary assessment of curb ramp condition and missing ramp needs. For
noncompliant curb ramps and missing ramps, the County may conduct detailed measurements
using a standardized measurement form to identify specific noncompliant elements and support
design scoping.

For implementation programming, curb ramp prioritization should consider both the
condition/severity of the curb ramp barrier and the importance of the crossing location in the
pedestrian network.


SIDEWALK PRIORITIZATION APPROACH
The Self-Evaluation Study describes a sidewalk scoring approach based on defect type and
severity. Sidewalk prioritization should consider defect severity, route continuity, and functional
importance, including whether the sidewalk segment is part of a primary pedestrian access route
to public facilities or services.

MONITORING, REPORTING, AND PLAN UPDATES
Ongoing monitoring and reporting support transparency and helps ensure that accessibility
improvements are integrated into transportation program delivery. Clark County Public Works
will maintain records of inventory updates, completed improvements, and unresolved barriers to
support plan maintenance and legal compliance documentation.


MONITORING ACTIVITIES
•   Maintain and update the pedestrian facility inventory in County records (including curb ramps,
    sidewalks, missing sidewalks, and pedestrian signal features).
•   Track completed ADA improvements through project closeout documentation and, where
    applicable, update inventory records to reflect corrected barriers.
•   Document MEF determinations and engineering constraints where full compliance cannot be
    achieved in an alteration project.
•   Maintain a log of public requests, complaints, and grievances related to public right-of-way
    accessibility and document responses and resolution status.
•   Coordinate with Countywide ADA program administration to ensure consistent public notice,
    effective communication, and grievance handling.


REPORTING AND PLAN UPDATES
Public Works should publish periodic progress summaries that describe completed improvements,
upcoming programmed projects, and updates to prioritization criteria or inventory methods. Plan
updates should occur as necessary to reflect material changes in inventory, funding, or regulatory
guidance. At a minimum, Public Works will update the Transportation ADA Transition Plan every
3-5 years per the guidelines.

CONCLUSION
This Transportation ADA Transition Plan provides Clark County Public Works with a structured
framework for identifying, prioritizing, and addressing accessibility barriers in the public right-of-
way pedestrian network. Implementation will occur over time through coordinated capital
projects, maintenance, and integration into transportation programming, guided by inventory data
and public input.
