APPENDICES

A P P E N D I X A — A DA S E L F – E V A L U A T I O N R E P O R T
Right of Way Self-Evaluation Study

Introduction/Purpose

The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) is a federal civil rights law that prohibits discrimination
against individuals with disabilities. Under Title II of the ADA 28 CFR 35.105, Clark County must
evaluate our "current services, policies and practices" to determine whether they comply with the
requirements of the ADA. This process is called self-evaluation. Clark County Public Works
developed this study to fulfill our self-evaluation requirements for pedestrian facilities within the
county public rights- of-way. This study does not address buildings, privately owned facilities, or
the facilities owned by the incorporated cities and towns of Clark County. Clark County is
committed to providing accessible pedestrian facilities which ensure that all our citizens have
access to our transportation system. This study identifies areas where the county must improve to
meet that commitment, and where the county is meeting it already.

Legal Requirements and Policies

An ADA Self-Evaluation Study and Transition Plan is a requirement for local governments based
on:

    •   Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) of 1990; and

    •   Washington State Department of Transportation (WSDOT) Local Agency Guidelines,
        Chapter 29.

State and local governments and public entities or agencies are required to perform a self-
evaluation of the County's current facilities, relative to the accessibility requirements of the
current ADA accessibility standards. The requirements of the ADA apply to all public entities or
agencies, no matter the size.

Transportation facilities in this study are those that make up the pedestrian access route and
pedestrian circulation path in the public right-of-way as defined in Clark County Code Title
40.350. Specifically, the types of facilities evaluated in this study will include curb ramps,
sidewalks, and traffic control signals. This study identifies barriers to the accessibility of these
facilities as defined by the ADA.




A PPENDIX L                                                                                            348
                                          CLARK2045
Self-Evaluation

As part of our self-evaluation, Clark County reviewed internal policies and practices related to
public rights-of-way accessibility. The county examined how they implement these policies and
practices and determined where modifications needed to be made to ensure accessibility.

The report contains a summary of the county's inventory of pedestrian facilities in the public right-
of-way. The inventory includes extensive measurements taken for each type of facility. The county
used the measurement data to determine what barriers to accessibility exist and how severe each
of those barriers is.

The County will conduct public outreach and involvement efforts to gain a better understanding
of the public's accessibility needs. The county will host public meetings and create website
materials. The information the county receives from our outreach efforts will help us gauge the
priorities of Clark County residents.

The transition plan lays out how and when the county will upgrade pedestrian facilities to achieve
compliance with the ADA requirements. This report is provided as an appendix to be periodically
updated as planned improvements are completed.

This document is being developed in accordance with federal requirements outlined in Section
504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 and in the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990.

Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973

Often referred to as the civil rights act for people with disabilities, the Rehabilitation Act requires
that all organizations receiving federal funding make their programs available to people of all
abilities. It states:

No otherwise qualified [disabled] individual in the United States shall, solely by reason of [disability], be
excluded from the participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any
program or activity receiving federal financial assistance.

Public agencies that receive federal funding must identify a Section 504 coordinator on its staff
who will ensure that the program, service, or activity receiving the funding meets the
requirements of the law and respond to any complaints from citizens or requests for information
from a funding agency.

Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) – Titles I and II

The U.S. Congress signed the ADA in 1990, and it went into effect in 1992. The ADA is a civil rights
law that prohibits discrimination against individuals with disabilities in access to jobs, public
accommodations, government services and programs, public transportation, and
telecommunications. The ADA consists of five titles:

• Title I: Employment

349                                                                                            A PPENDIX L
                                      CLARK2045
• Title II: State and Local Government

• Title III: Public Accommodations and Commercial Facilities

• Title IV: Telecommunications

• Title V: Miscellaneous



Title I of the ADA prohibits private employers, state and local governments, employment agencies,
and labor unions from discriminating against qualified individuals with disabilities in job
application procedures, hiring, firing, advancement, compensation, job training, and other terms,
conditions, and privileges of employment. Clark County is an Equal Employment Opportunity
(EEO) employer and adheres to the requirements of Title I.

Title II of the ADA adopts the general prohibitions against discrimination contained in Section 504
of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 but applies to all state and local governments, regardless of
whether or not they receive federal funding. It prohibits Clark County from denying persons with
disabilities the equal opportunity to participate in its services, programs, or activities, either
directly or indirectly through contractual arrangements.

The administrative requirements contained in Title II that apply to CLARK COUNTY are:

• Designation of an ADA Coordinator responsible for overseeing Title II compliance;

• Developing and posting an ADA Notice to the Public;

• Development of an ADA complaint procedure;

• Completion of a self-evaluation of facilities, programs, and services; and

• Development of a program access plan if the self-evaluation identifies any accessibility
deficiencies.




A PPENDIX L                                                                                   350
                                           CLARK2045
Individuals with Disabilities

The American Community Survey (ACS) administered by the US Census Bureau adopted several
disability-related questions since 2000. These questions cover the following six disability types:

1. Hearing difficulty: deaf or having serious difficulty hearing

2. Vision difficulty: blind or having serious difficulty seeing, even when wearing glasses

3. Cognitive difficulty: because of a physical, mental, or emotional problem, having difficulty
remembering, concentrating, or making decisions

4. Ambulatory difficulty: having serious difficulty walking or climbing stairs

5. Self-care difficulty: having difficulty bathing or dressing

6. Independent living difficulty: because of a physical, mental, or emotional problem, having
difficulty doing errands alone, such as visiting a doctor's office or shopping

Policies and Procedures

This section contains a review of Clark County policies and procedures with relation to the ADA.
As a result of the review, the county found some policies as practices were adequately addressed
to ensure ADA compliance. The county determined that other policies may need revisions and
identified areas where the county needed to develop new policies. As new information becomes
available, or ADA standards change, the county will update our policies and practices to
incorporate the latest information and standards.

Existing Policies and Procedures Deemed Adequate

Clark County found the following policies and practice to be adequate to ensure compliance with
the ADA:

   •   Clark County Grievance Procedure under the Americans with Disabilities Act: The
       grievance procedures are used to file a complaint alleging discrimination based on
       disability in the provisions of services, activities, programs, or benefits by Clark County.
       Information on the county's grievance process can be found on the county's website, or by
       contacting the Clark County ADA Coordinator.

   •   Congestion and Safety Management: Public Works administers a congestion and safety
       management system commonly referred to as concurrency.

   •   Clark County Pedestrian Crossing Prioritization Program (PCPP): The PCPP was
       developed to provide a process that identifies priority locations for implementing new or
       enhanced pedestrian crossings. The recommended prioritization process follows national
       practices related to identifying pedestrian crossing locations and the County's pedestrian
       crossing guidance and practices. This study describes the PCPP framework for evaluating
       potential locations for crossing enhancements and outlines the screening process the
       County developed to identify and review locations.

   •   Clark County Code, 12.26, Sidewalk Maintenance and Repair: Requires property owners
       to keep sidewalks along their property in good order and repair. Public Works typically
       receives maintenance requests through its online maintenance request form. When
       sidewalk concerns are received, Public Works will verify the sidewalk defects through an
       inspection and mark the defects with paint. Adjacent property owners will be sent a letter
       informing them of the code and their responsibility. Replacement or modifications to
       existing sidewalk or approaches that impact public right-of-way requires an APS permit
       through Clark County Community Development.



   •   Clark County Annual ADA Curb Ramp Compliance Projects: Each year Public Works
       Transportation Section will have annual maintenance projects. These projects include the
       Hot Mix Asphalt (HMA) overlay on some of our roads that need to be maintained.
       However, the annual ADA projects will replace or install between 100 -200 curb ramps per

A PPENDIX L                                                                                    352
                                      CLARK2045
       year. These ramps are replaced where intersections will be paved in the following with the
       HMA project.

   •   Clark County Public Works Sidewalk and ADA Ongoing Program: This program focuses on
       the Clark County Public Works Transportation Section’s ongoing efforts for sidewalks and
       ADA improvements. These efforts are designed to facilitate smaller infill, retrofit or ‘spot’
       improvements in established locations throughout the county.

New and Modified Policies and Practices to Be Developed

ADA Ramp Ranking System: This is a method being used to rank the ADA ramps in Clark County
which would help with prioritizing which ramps should be corrected first.

County Information and Ramp Evaluation

How did the County inventory ADA barriers across its facilities, programs, services, and activities?

The County has inventoried barriers since 2011. Majority of the inventory collected was curb
ramps and sidewalks. Additional work is needed to inventory ramped driveways and pedestrian
signal lights, along with updating curb ramps, and sidewalk data.

Pedestrian Facility Inventory

In 2019, the county provided an inventory of the following existing pedestrian facilities, curb
ramps, sidewalks, and traffic signals with Assessable Pedestrian Signals (APS). This was the major
component of the self-evaluation process. The county measured thousands of facilities across the
county. The data collected allows us to determine whether any individual facility meets ADA
requirements. The county can then use the information to quantify the severity of defects which
impact a facility's accessibility. An understanding of existing defects, combined with priorities
expressed by the public, will ultimately serve as the basis to identify and prioritize locations that
need accessibility improvements. The prioritization method and schedule to complete
improvements will be included in our forthcoming ADA Transition Plan for Public Rights-of-Way.
The county designed our inventory system to assess existing pedestrian facilities compliance with
all design standards in 2023 PROWAG.

Inventory Findings

This section includes a quantitative summary of measurements taken for each type of pedestrian
facility Clark County inventoried. These statistics are intended to help assess the state of our
entire network of public right-of-way pedestrian facilities. The statistical categories generally
cover just one type of measurement, but the inventory data can be analyzed according to any
combination of different measurements. The statistics show the percentages of facilities that are
ADA compliant in each measurement category, as well as several non-compliant ranges to show
how far from compliance some facilities are.




353                                                                                     A PPENDIX L
                                     CLARK2045
Many facilities that are fully ADA compliant in one measurement category are non-compliant in
another. The forthcoming ADA Transition Plan for Public Rights-of-Way will address all the
facilities that are non-compliant in at least one measurement category.

Curb Ramps

Clark County located and measured curb ramps in all locations where sidewalks were in the public
right-of-way. Each curb ramp required a combination of up to 36 different measurements and
observations. Curb ramp data includes many measurements of elements beyond the ramp itself.
The county measured and recorded data for elements such as turning space, clear space, gutters,
crosswalks, flared sides, and detectable warning surfaces for each ramp. In many instances a single
ramp will include measurements for two ramps on the same corner in two directions or two
crosswalks. The county also noted locations where curb ramps are required to serve a legal
crossing of a public road but are currently absent. The county recorded these as missing ramps.

Clark County measured 9,500+ curb ramp locations. Figure 1 below shows the locations of all curb

below is an up-close view of the locations from what was inspected and inventoried. Table 2 is the

New ramps are identified using the ADA Curb Ramp Improvement Projects. The ADA
Improvement Projects will deliver important infrastructure upgrades, including:

      •   Curb ramp construction and upgrades including the addition of detectable warning
          surfaces to guide visually impaired pedestrians and improve accessibility in compliance

associated with it. The MEF documentation is stored in Public Works Engineering and Design
project files. This data will be added manually to the data set.

This system is a subjective method of rating and is currently being phased out to be replaced with
a more objective method similar to WSDOT ADA Measurement Form, 2018 that measures many
of the ramp features and ramp/roadway interface.

Currently, an attribute column needs to be added to the county’s GIS layer. The PM in charge of
the ADA ramp reconstruction project will have a list of different ramps listed by the Facility ID.
This list will be given to GIS and the data uploaded via script.




40
     Photo of Clark County GIS 2019

357                                                                                    A PPENDIX L
                                     CLARK2045
The ramps are rated 1-6 using a method developed by Public Works Engineering and Design
section. The system is as follows:

       1. All Elements Compliant

       2. Compliant, Domes Missing

       3. Steep Slopes, Noncompliant

       4. One or Two elements Noncompliant

       5. Three or more elements Noncompliant

       6. No ramp but one required



Currently, there is an effort to collect additional ramp data per the WSDOT ADA Measurement
Form, 2018. Teams of two will go out and collect the additional measurements using an iPad and
the Collector app. These additional measurements will be used to rate and prioritize future ramp
replacement projects.

For example, in the 2026 HMA and Cape Seal areas, 39% of the ramps had been measured at the
time of the vetting process. Due to the low number of measurements, the vetting process mostly
relied on the qualitative visual inspection method established prior to 2025. When ramp
measurements were taken and data was available a pass/no pass method was used for each ramp
measurement.



Sidewalks

Sidewalks form the backbone of Clark County's pedestrian transportation network in the urban
areas of the county. The sidewalks measured for this plan were only those within county owned
roadway right-of-way. Paths at parks, or sidewalks along private roadways were not included,
because they are not within the jurisdiction of Clark County Public Works Transportation.

The county measured all sidewalks according to the procedures contained in Figure 3 and 4 below.
Some of the attributes measured were sidewalk width, cross slope, and condition. The condition
rating addresses maintenance issues that surface over time, such as cracked panels, lifted panels,
and vegetation encroachment.

In 2018-2019 majority of the sidewalks in the County had been inventoried.

Using data from the sidewalk layer, GIS created an inverse map, which shows where sidewalks are
missing. These features are then scored using the Sidewalk Program, the weighted scoring which
is based on the roadway classification, destination, and quality of life criteria.

Public Works review potential locations of defective sidewalks using a scoring process that
includes pedestrian accident history, nearby housing density, road width, speed limit and sight-
distance limitations caused by hills and curves. Distance to schools, stores, shopping, medical
offices, bus stops, and other destinations also are considered. This does not include missing
sidewalks. Photo #2, depicts a sidewalk that has vertical displacement, thus being out of
compliance with ADA standards.

Top-scoring sidewalks are reviewed for potential conflicts with upcoming county road projects or
private development proposals. Technical concerns, such as the need for additional right of way,
environmental regulations and construction challenges, are also examined to determine when
walkways will be built.

Traffic Signals

Traffic signals are an important part of the county's transportation system. They play a critical role
in the pedestrian network by assisting pedestrians in safely navigating intersections. The county
traffic signal inventory included measurements of the pedestrian features of every traffic signal
system in the public right-of-way. Photo #4 below illustrates what would be a non-compliant push
button system in the public right-of-way.




42
     Source: Clark County GIS Department 2019

367                                                                                     A PPENDIX L
                                    CLARK2045
Photo 4: Non-Compliant Accessible Pushbutton Signal




Pedestrian push buttons were the primary features of signal systems which Clark County
measured and evaluated for accessibility. The county measured the height of the center of the
buttons above the ground and the distances between buttons on corners where there are two
buttons for separate directions of the crosswalk. The county also measured the distances from
buttons to the bottom of curb ramps. Lastly, the county evaluated the buttons themselves to
determine whether they comply with ADA standards for accessible pedestrian signals (APS) as
detailed in the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD). According to standards in
the MUTCD buttons must relay audible messages, contain tactile information, and be easy to
activate. The county measured 101 pedestrian push button signal locations and 99 of them are
ADA compliant. The maps make no distinction between buttons that are compliant and those that
are non-compliant.

The Public Works Traffic Signal Section is currently collecting light pole data adjacent to
crosswalk to complete a lighting analysis. Photo #5 shows what a properly functioning APS system
looks like, while Photo #6 is a properly installed APS.




A PPENDIX L                                                                                368
                                      CLARK2045
Photo 5: ADA Accessible Pushbuttons (APS)




The objective is to map all the signal poles and lighting poles that the County maintains and pays
the electricity bill. The data would be used for asset management as well as an auditing feature to
reconcile the County power bill.

98% of all county pedestrians push buttons include ADA compliant APS features. APS buttons
include audio and vibrating tactile information. This information ensures that people who are
blind, or have low vision, get the same crossing information available to people with unimpaired
vision. The county has adopted a policy, included in the Policies and Practices section of this
report, which details when an alteration to a Clark County signal system requires the installation
of new pedestrian push buttons with APS.

Clark County will address all pedestrian signals identified above that are not ADA compliant in the
ADA Transition Plan. The ADA Transition Plan will lay out how and when the county will make
pedestrian signals accessible to achieve compliance with the ADA.

Public Involvement and Outreach

As part of the self-evaluation process Clark County made significant efforts to reach out to people
with disabilities and those who represent them. The county held two open house events in
different areas of unincorporated Clark County. The county will reach out to organizations that
serve individuals with disabilities and offer to meet with their members.

The county made all materials available on the county’s website at www.clark.wa/ADAtransition
and provided an opportunity for the public to participate through an online survey and online
comments. A more comprehensive summary of our public outreach efforts is included in this
document.

Public Meetings and Organization Meetings

Clark County held two separate public meetings on the following dates and locations:

           •   Prairie High School, 11311 NE 119th St., Vancouver, WA 98662, November 20th,
               2025;



A PPENDIX L                                                                                   370
                                      CLARK2045
           •   Felida Elementary School, 2700 NW 119th St., Vancouver, WA 98685 January 22nd,
               2026.

The meetings included a presentation about the county efforts to complete the Self-Evaluation
Report and ADA Transition Plan for Public Rights-of-Way followed by time for questions and
answers.

Conclusions

The detailed findings of this report make it clear that there are deficiencies in many existing
pedestrian facilities in Clark County’s public rights-of-way. These deficiencies create significant
barriers to access for many community members with disabilities.

Clark County is committed to creating a more accessible pedestrian transportation network for all
members of the community. To address the deficiencies identified in this report, Clark County is
currently developing an ADA Transition Plan for Public Rights-of-Way. Title II of the Americans
with Disabilities Act 28 CFR 35.150(d) sets forth the requirements for this plan. This plan will
identify noncompliant pedestrian facilities that limit accessibility, describe how these barriers to
access will be corrected, specify a schedule for achieving compliance, and designate an official
responsible for implementing the plan.


A P P E N D I X B — AD A G R I E V A N C E P R O C E D U R E
This appendix summarizes Clark County’s ADA grievance procedure for public access. The
grievance procedure is maintained by the County ADA Coordinator and is available on the Clark
County website. In the event of any discrepancy between this appendix and the County’s posted
procedure, the posted procedure controls.

Purpose. The grievance procedure provides a means for residents to file complaints regarding: (1)
Clark County policies or the provision of services, activities, and programs to persons with
disabilities; (2) alleged discrimination in the provision of services, activities, and programs under
Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973; and (3) structural and parking accessibility issues on
County-owned or controlled property.

B.1 GRIEVANCE PROCEDURE AND FORMAT
A complainant should provide their name, address, phone number, and the location, date, and
description of the problem. Alternate means of filing complaints (such as personal interviews or a
tape recording) will be made available for persons with disabilities upon request.

B.2 GRIEVANCE FILING
A complainant and/or their designee should submit the complaint as soon as possible but no later
than 60 calendar days after the alleged violation to:

•   Michelle Schuster Clark County ADA Coordinator


371                                                                                     A PPENDIX L
                                       CLARK2045
•   Internal Services
•   1300 Franklin Street, Sixth Floor
•   Vancouver, WA 98660
•   Main phone: 564-397-2282
•   TTY: 800-833-6388 or Relay Service 711
•   Speech-to-Speech Relay: 877-833-6341
•   Email: ADA@clark.wa.gov

B.3 GRIEVANCE REVIEW
Within 15 calendar days after receipt of the complaint, the ADA Coordinator (or Human
Resources representative for employment-related matters) will meet with or contact the
complainant to review and clarify the issues. Within 30 calendar days of the initial meeting, the
County will provide a response in writing or in an accessible format, explaining the County’s
position and/or offering options for resolution or mediation.

B.4 GRIEVANCE APPEAL PROCESS
If the initial response does not satisfactorily resolve the issue, the complainant and/or their
designee may appeal the decision within 15 calendar days after receipt of the County’s response
to the Clark County Manager. Within 15 calendar days after receipt of the appeal, the County
Manager (or designee) will meet with the complainant to discuss the complaint and possible
resolutions and will respond in writing (or in an accessible format) with a final resolution within 15
calendar days after the initial meeting.

B.5 GRIEVANCE RECORD RETENTION
Written complaints, appeals, and responses will be retained by Clark County for at least three
years.

Additional options. If a satisfactory resolution is not reached, the complainant may elect to file a
federal complaint or pursue other means of resolution consistent with applicable law(s).

C.1 PUBLIC NOTICE TEMPLATE
Clark County does not discriminate on the basis of disability in the provision of services, activities,
and programs. In accordance with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), Clark County will
provide reasonable accommodations for qualified individuals with disabilities. To request
accommodations or to obtain information in an alternate format, contact the Clark County ADA
Coordinator.

APPENDIX E — INVENTORY METHODOLOGY SUMMARY
This appendix summarizes the inventory and self-evaluation methodology described in the Clark
County Right of Way Self-Evaluation Study. The intent is to document how barriers were
identified and evaluated to support transparency and repeatability.

E.1 DATA SOURCES AND TOOLS
•     GIS-based pedestrian facility inventory layers maintained by Clark County (including curb
      ramps, sidewalks, and missing sidewalk segments).
•     Curb ramp visual inspection ranking (Ranks 1–6) used as a screening tool.
•     Detailed curb ramp measurement using standardized measurement forms (including the
      WSDOT ADA Curb Ramp Measurement Form, 2018, as described in the Self-Evaluation
      Study).
•     Sidewalk defect identification and scoring based on defect type and severity.
•     Pedestrian pushbutton and APS measurement at signalized locations evaluated.

APPENDIX M
Racially Disparate Impacts Analysis

BACKGROUND

LEGISLATIVE REQUIREMENTS
In 2021, the Washington State Legislature changed the planning requirements for housing
through House Bill 1220 (HB 1220). The updated statute in RCW 36.70A.020(4) strengthened the
Growth Management Act (GMA) housing goal from “encourage affordable housing” to “plan for
and accommodate” housing affordable to all income levels. Local governments now must go
beyond simply encouraging affordable housing and must actively “plan for and accommodate
housing” affordable to all economic segments of the community.

In addition, the updated statute in RCW 36.70A.070(2) requires jurisdictions to address zoning
that may have a racially disparate or exclusionary effect and address patterns of disinvestment.
Local governments must also identify displacement risk and establish policies to prevent
displacement or reduce the hardships caused by displacement.

Specifically, the new requirements in RCW 36.70A.070(2) state that jurisdictions must now adopt
a housing element that:

       (e) Identifies local policies and regulations that result in racially disparate impacts, displacement,
       and exclusion in housing, including: (i) Zoning that may have a discriminatory effect; (ii)
       Disinvestment; and (iii) Infrastructure availability;

       (f) Identifies and implements policies and regulations to address and begin to undo racially
       disparate impacts, displacement, and exclusion in housing caused by local policies, plans, and
       actions;

       (g) Identifies areas that may be at higher risk of displacement from market forces that occur with
       changes to zoning development regulations and capital investments; and

       (h) Establishes anti-displacement policies, with consideration given to the preservation of
       historical and cultural communities as well as investments in low, very low, extremely low, and
       moderate-income housing; equitable development initiatives; inclusionary zoning; community
       planning requirements; tenant protections; land disposition policies; and consideration of land
       that may be used for affordable housing.

The new requirements are not a statement against current communities in which there are racially
disparate outcomes in housing, but an acknowledgement of the role land use policy has played in

A PPENDIX M                                                                                              388
                                      CLARK2045
creating and institutionalizing race-based advantages and disadvantages. The statute uses the
term “racially disparate” but does not identify protected groups based on race.

The Washington Department of Commerce (Commerce) Guidance (guidance) to Address Racially
Disparate Impacts provides local jurisdictions guidance on updating housing elements to address
the new requirements related to racially disparate impacts, exclusion in housing, displacement,
and areas at high risk of displacement in the future.

DEFINITIONS
HB 1220 added new terms in the housing element statute with subsections e-h above. Commerce
guidance includes definitions of key terms from the statute, including:

   •   Displacement: The process by which a household is forced to move from its community
       because of conditions beyond their control.
           o Physical displacement: Households are directly forced to move for reasons such as
               eviction, foreclosure, natural disaster or deterioration in housing quality.
           o Economic displacement: Households are compelled to move by rising rents or costs
               of home ownership like property taxes.
           o Cultural displacement: Residents are compelled to move because the people and
               institutions that make up their cultural community have left the area.
   •   Displacement risk: The likelihood that a household, business or organization will be
       displaced from its community.
   •   Exclusion in housing: The act or effect of shutting or keeping certain populations out of
       housing within a specified area, in a manner that may be intentional or unintentional, but
       which leads to non-inclusive impacts.
   •   Racially disparate impacts: When policies, practices, rules or other systems result in a
       disproportionate impact on one or more racial groups.

METHODOLOGY
Clark County’s methodology included: community engagement and a series of procedural steps
including: a data assessment, audit of housing element goals, policies, strategies and associated
development regulations, goal/policy/strategy/regulation revisions to address audit findings, and
a consistency review.


COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT
Clark County’s comprehensive plan community engagement relating to racial health disparities
builds on previous county initiatives. Clark County conducted a Housing Options Study and Action
Plan that was adopted in 2022. This project included a public participation plan with goals to focus
social justice and equity, accessible participation, meaningful participation, transparency and
accountability and included a project advisory group representing a wide range of interests and
perspectives, including a dedicated position to help advise the county from a perspective of


389                                                                                  A PPENDIX M
                                     CLARK2045
housing access for populations disproportionally affected by systems of racism and oppression, as
well as representatives of additional marginalized groups.

Additional recent Clark County community engagement initiatives outside of the Community
Planning Department relate to the intersection of systemic racism and housing. Examples of these
initiatives include: the 2020 Clark County Community Needs Assessment, the Clark County
Affordable Housing Planning Committee convened by the Community Services Department to
address the rapidly escalating affordable housing crisis, and the Public Health 2023 Clark County
Community Health Assessment (CHA) and Community Health Improvement Plan (CHIP).

The Comprehensive Plan racially disparate impacts analysis work builds on these previous
initiatives and followed the Public Participation Plan developed for the comprehensive plan
update process. Some examples of how the county identified and engaged with communities in the
county that may be experiencing disparate impacts, exclusion or displacement include:

   o   The county engaged with thousands of community members, including individuals who
       identify as BIPOC and organizations who serve communities of color, including several
       Clark County community based organizations that received comprehensive plan
       community engagement grants from the Department of Commerce.
   o   As part of the implementation work of the Housing Options Study and Action Plan and
       housing code work for the comprehensive plan update, the county facilitated multiple
       housing forum discussions. Forum members’ purpose is to discuss proposed code concepts
       and code language with stakeholders who have familiarity with Clark County Title 40
       and/or development (housing) regulations. This group includes representatives from the
       Vancouver Housing Authority and Housing Initiative, a subsidiary of the Council for the
       Homeless.
   o   The county facilitated an Environmental Justice Coalition, made up of 15 community-
       based organizations who serve populations vulnerable to the impacts of climate change.
       These organizations helped the county with its engagement for its new Climate Element,
       some of which related to the intersection of racial disparities, resilience, and housing.


PROCESS
Clark County used the following process for assessing racially disparate impacts, exclusion in
housing, displacement, and areas at high risk of displacement in the future.

   1. Gather and analyze data
         a. Review previous data analysis conducted for Clark County in the Clark County
             Housing Options Study and Action Plan and other county housing and racial equity
             reports and projects.
         b. Review resources recommended in the Commerce guidance
   2. Evaluate comprehensive plan housing element goals, policies, strategies, and associated
      development regulations based on Commerce guidance

DATA AND HISTORY
Multiple data sources were reviewed for the Clark County unincorporated urban and rural areas
to help assess racially disparate impacts, exclusion in housing, displacement, and areas at high risk
of displacement in the future. A summary of data sources reviewed and key findings follows.


HISTORICAL CONTEXT

CLARK COUNTY LISTENING SESSIONS AND RESOLUTIONS
On June 16, 2020, the Clark County Council adopted a resolution to work towards eliminating
systemic racism and injustice in Clark County [Resolution No. 2020-06-06]. Over the summer of
that year, the Clark County Council and YWCA Clark County, NAACP Vancouver, Southwest
Washington LULAC, and Clark County Volunteer Lawyers Program held several listening sessions
to learn about how systemic racism has impacted residents of Clark County. 43 On December 1,
2020, the Clark County Council took the additional step and adopted a resolution to eliminate
systemic racism and health inequities [Resolution No. 2020-12-05]. The listening session
presentations were wide ranging, and a few have a direct impact on the historic settlement
patterns of Clark County.

Dispossession of Native Lands
Supreme Court decision Johnson v M’Intoch (1823) establishes the “discovery doctrine” that
allowed those who “discovered” land to extinguish the “right of occupancy” over native American
lands. The legal result is that only native American conveyances of land to the federal government
create valid title. The result was the purchase of native American borderlands for pennies on the
dollar which allowed for the creation of settlements on the purchased lands and spurs the western
migration with subsidized land transfers. The spreading of disease by settlers killed Native
Americans and the clearing of the land made it less valuable to the Native Americans. Clark
County is located within the ancestral territory of the Chinook, Klickitat and Cowlitz People,
among other tribes.

Oregon Terri tory Laws
In the early 1840s several laws were passed by the governing body of the Oregon Territory that
amended the 1787 Northwest Ordinance banning slavery. The Burnett Leash set a time frame for
a free Black person to leave the state or be subject to a lashing and the Black Exclusion Law
specified that “it shall not be lawful for any negro or mulatto to enter into, or reside” in Oregon,
with exceptions made for those who were already in the territory. While these laws were rarely
enforced the intended effect was to discourage a black person from settling in the Oregon
Territory.

Wartime Migra tion
Before 1940 Clark County had few residents who were black. World War II brought thousands of
Black workers to the Kaiser Shipyard in Vancouver, raising the African American population to
nearly 9,000 by 1944. In mid-1945, 57% of black families surveyed planned to “definitely to
remain in the Vancouver area.”

“Now that the war is over, you people can go home,” is how it felt to Joseph H. Bailey, a Black
shipyard worker interviewed later by The Columbian.

The city’s African American population plummeted from nearly 9,000 in 1940 to just 440 in 1960,
according to the Civil Rights and Labor History Consortium at the University of Washington.

Racially Restrictiv e Covenants 44
From the 1920s through the early 1940s there is evidence of racially restrictive covenants being
placed on subdivisions within Clark County. Example of the language in the covenants:

        “No race or nationality other than those of the Caucasian or White race shall occupy and
        dwelling on any lot except this covenant shall not prevent occupancy by domestic servants
        of a different race or nationality employed by an owner or tenant.”

        “The property and/or improvements thereon shall not be owned or occupied by anyone
        other than a member of the white race.”

Although the 1948 Supreme Court Decision declared the covenants unenforceable, it yielded
little power and the Fair Housing Act of 1968 made the covenants illegal.

Research done by the University of Washington contains maps where racial restrictions were
added to property records in the decades before 1968. Most restrictions in Clark County date from
1926 to 1952 and covered a substantial percentage of subdivisions. The University of Washington
project identified more than 1,367 properties in 34 subdivisions and concludes that restrictive
covenants were only one of the mechanisms of segregation; that neighborhoods without covenants

often practiced racial exclusion by other means. While most of the properties are in the current
boundaries of the City of Vancouver some are in the unincorporated urban area in: Minnehaha
(Truman Neighborhood), Highway 99 Subarea (Felida/Sherwood Neighborhoods), and Barberton
area. Over time the census tracts where these properties are located have also become the location

In 2019 Clark County began a process to create a Housing Options Study and Action Plan
(HOSAP). The objective was to provide information regarding the local housing market and
identify barriers that exist in providing a greater variety of housing types. As part of the HOSAP
development, a housing inventory and analysis was conducted. 49 Data from this report focuses on
the unincorporated Vancouver Urban Growth Area (referred to as the Study Area in the report)
and, at times, all of Clark County. Excerpted findings from the report include:

     •   The racial composition of Clark County, WA today has a majority White racial group. The
         unincorporated Vancouver Urban Growth Area’s racial composition is similar to the racial
         composition of the countywide Clark County population.
     •   The largest racial minority group in Clark County and the unincorporated Vancouver
         Urban Growth Area are residents who identify as Hispanic or Latino of any race.
     •   Groups that identified as Black and Some Other Race have a comparatively lower median
         household income (MHI) than groups of other races and ethnicities in the unincorporated
         Vancouver Urban Growth Area.

Environ menta l Hea lth Disparities 53
The Washington State Department of Health developed an environmental health disparities map
that shows the relative burden of each census tract in the state related to 25 environmental and
socioeconomic factors. A copy of the WA Environmental Health Disparities (EHD) map (version
3.0) for Clark County is provided in Comprehensive Plan Figure 37. Based on this map, the most
burdened census tracts in the unincorporated county are located in the Hazel Dell, Minnehaha,
and Five Corners/Orchards areas. 54, 55

The Environmental Health Disparities map is consistent with local Clark County Public Health
research. For instance, Clark County Public Health Prioritizing Places, 2024, Clark County
Community Health Assessment, and 2024-2029 Clark County Community Health Improvement
Plan (CHIP) all use a health lens to, respectively, identify priority places in the community with
poor health outcomes, identify priority community health needs, and identify ways to improve
health outcomes. The findings from these projects align with the information illustrated in the
environmental health disparities map.

The Environmental Health Disparities Map allows viewers to look at individual factors. When
comparing the percent of people of color by census tract to the location of the most burdened
census tracts, the census tracts with the highest percentage of people of color in Clark County
tend to overlap with highly burdened census tracts.

         people who are experiencing poverty in this community. Though there are more white
         people who struggle financially in Clark County, in comparison to their overall numbers
         BIPOC communities are disproportionately experiencing poverty.
     •   Survey respondents were asked to identify the top five service area needs for their family.
         Almost one half (49%) of respondents identified housing assistance as their most
         important need.

Bridging the Gap: Evaluating Chall en ges and Opportuni ties for
Afforda ble Housing Solu tions in Clark County 58
Over the past decade, Clark County, Washington, has faced a rapidly escalating affordable
housing crisis. The Clark County Affordable Housing Planning Committee was convened to
address this issue, bringing together stakeholders from across sectors-including housing
developers, government agencies, community organizations, and residents – to collaboratively
develop actional strategies. A report was written to summarize the findings and recommendations
of the committee. Excerpts from those findings include:

     •   People of color represent a disproportionate share of the homeless population, despite
         only making up approximately 25% of the general population. The 2024 Point in Time (PIT)
         count revealed that 39% of the county’s unhoused population identified as Black,
         Indigenous, or People of Color (BIPOC), despite BIPOC individuals only making up 25% of
         the general population.
     •   People of color are more likely to experience housing instability due to lower rates of
         home ownership, limited access to affordable housing, and higher rates of eviction. This
         disparity in access often leads to cycles of homelessness and housing insecurity.
     •   Economic inequities: economic challenges, including wage stagnation and rising housing
         costs, have disproportionately affected lower-income and marginalized communities,
         exacerbating housing insecurity and homelessness.

poverty rates and the houseless population in the county, in alignment with other county housing

FINDINGS
The following key findings are based on review of the above information:

   •   Clark County, WA is located in a place with a history that includes dispossession of native
       lands, black exclusion laws, discrimination against African Americans, and racially
       restrictive covenants.
   •   In more recent years, some Clark County, WA some residents have report having
       experienced with racial bias/discrimination.
   •   A higher percentage of White and Asian racial groups own homes compared to other racial
       groups.
   •   A higher percentage of Pacific Islander, Black or African American, and Hispanic or Latino
       racial groups rent homes compared to other racial groups.
   •   People of color are overrepresented among those who have experienced poverty and who
       have experienced houselessness.
   •   People of color are more likely to experience housing instability due to lower rates of
       home ownership, limited access to affordable housing, and higher rates of eviction.
   •   There is a higher proportion of cost burdened households among Hispanic/Latino and
       Black or African American racial groups. There is a lower rate of cost burden among White
       and Asian racial groups.
   •   Black and Some other Race racial groups that have disproportionately lower household
       incomes would be disproportionately impacted by an insufficient amount of affordable,
       multifamily housing options in unincorporated Clark County.
   •   Pacific Islander, Black or African American, and Hispanic or Latino racial groups that have
       a disproportionate amount of households that rent housing would be disproportionately
       impacted by an insufficient amount of affordable, multifamily housing options in
       unincorporated Clark County.
   •   The most overburdened census tracts according to the Washington State Environmental
       Health Disparities map in the unincorporated county are located in the Hazel Dell,
       Minnehaha, and Five Corners/Orchards areas. Census tracts with the highest percentages
       of people of color living in unincorporated Clark County are also located within the
       Minnehaha and Orchards areas.
   •   The census tracts with properties with racially restricted covenants share the same census
       tracts with several multi family housing developments. Two of the three areas share the
       same census tracts as areas with a high risk of displacement (Comprehensive Plan Figure
       35) and two share census tracks considered to be highly impacted, meaning they have a
       relatively high environmental health disparities rank in the WA State Environmental Health
       Disparities Map (Comprehensive Plan Figure 37). Today, these census tracts also have some
       of the highest percentages of people of color living in unincorporated Clark County,
       between 29-35%, indicating an increase in racially diverse households living in these census
       tracts since the racially restricted covenants were in effect.
   •   There is an imbalance between job and housing opportunities in terms of who lives and
       who works in Clark County. Most people who live in the unincorporated Vancouver Urban
       Growth Area commute out of the area for work. A majority of the people working in the

A PPENDIX M                                                                                   400
                                        CLARK2045
         unincorporated Vancouver Urban Growth Area commute into the area for work. This
         indicates that both higher wage jobs in the county and more affordable housing options in
         the county are needed.

Impediments to Fa ir Housing Choice
In 2012, Clark County Community Services published a report on Analysis of Impediments to Fair
Housing Choice as a mandated review by the US Department of Housing & Urban Development
(HUD). 60 The report and HUD defined impediments to fair housing choice as:

     o   Any actions, omissions, or decisions taken because of race, color, religion, sex, disability,
         familial status or national origin that restrict housing choices or the availability of housing
         choices.
     o   Any actions, omissions or decisions that have the effect of restricting housing choices or
         the availability of housing choices on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, disability,
         familial status or national origin.




60
  Source: Analysis of Impediments to Fair Housing Choice. Clark County, Washington. June 1, 2012.
https://clark.wa.gov/sites/default/files/dept/files/community-services/CDBG/FullAIReport.pdf

401                                                                                       A PPENDIX M
                                     CLARK2045
The report found few fair housing concerns and many positive fair housing practices within the
county. Some findings from the report include:

   •   Few concentrated areas. An analysis of racial and ethnic concentrations found very few
       Census tracts in the county with higher than average proportions of minorities. The areas
       with higher-than-average minority populations are almost all located in Vancouver.
   •   The dissimilarity index-a measure of the “evenness” of the geographic distribution of two
       different population groups-in Clark County is low, although higher than in Vancouver.
       The index ranges from 0 to 1, with a value of 1 representing full concentration. Clark
       County’s dissimilarity indexes where 0.20 (White v. Non-White comparison), 0.22 (Non-
       Hispanic v. Hispanic), 0.27 (White V. Asian) and 0.28 (White v. African American).
   •   Low volume of complaints and legal cases.

Opportunities to improve fair housing conditions in Clark County included:

   •   Stakeholders perceive a lack of transit options for low income, disabled and senior
       residents as a fair housing barrier. In addition to income levels and poor credit histories,
       stakeholders rated the lack of transit options for low income, disabled and senior residents
       as very high.
   •   Rental costs are high and Vancouver has a disproportionate number of subsidized rental
       units. An examination of the geographic location of the county’s public housing units and
       other subsidized housing found that two-thirds are located within one zip code. There are
       few affordable housing developments outside of Vancouver and its immediate environs.
   •   Hispanic, and to a lesser extent, Asian mortgage loan applicants are denied loans at much
       higher rates than Whites. Although the number of mortgage loan transactions is small
       relative to the county overall, in Battle Ground, Camas and La Center, Hispanic and Asian
       applicants were denied loans at much higher rates than White applicants.

FINDINGS
The following findings are based on review of the above information:

   •   Unincorporated Clark County’s history includes housing exclusion practices including:
       dispossession of native lands, black exclusion laws, discrimination against African, racially
       restrictive covenants, and zoning restricted for single-household dwellings.
   •   The 2012 Analysis of Impediments to Fair Housing Choice found few fair housing concerns
       and many positive fair housing practices within the county.
   •   Clark County is heavily automobile-dependent. A lack of transit options for low income,
       disabled and senior residents can be a fair housing barrier.
   •   Disproportionate mortgage lending practices for Hispanic and Asian racial groups have
       been reported in Clark County.
   •   The City of Vancouver has a disproportionate higher number of the county’s subsidized
       rental units, particularly zip code 98661, compared to other county jurisdictions. This zip
       code is partially located in the City of Vancouver and partially located in the
       unincorporated Vancouver Urban Growth Area.

ASSESSING DISPLACEMENT

RESOURCES REVIEWED

Historical Conte xt
See above for discussion of this topic.

Foreclosures
Foreclosure sales in Washington are noticed, scheduled, and conducted at the county level. As of
September 15, 2026, Clark County was the fifth busiest of the 32 Washington counties tracked,
holding 6.6% of the state’s tracked foreclosure inventory. Clark County is also the fifth most
populous county in Washington. 61

Evictions
Clark County has had the highest number of evictions per capita in Washington state for three
consecutive years which has been tied to the widening gap between residents’ incomes and rental
costs with limited rental assistance availability. 62

FINDINGS
The following findings are based on review of the above information:

     •   Clark County homeowners have not seemed to be at a disproportionately higher risk of
         foreclosure than homeowners in other counties in Washington State.
     •   Renters, particularly those in lower income households, have been displaced at a
         disproportionately higher rate in Clark County than other counties in Washington state
         due to the widening gap between residents’ incomes and rental costs with limited rental
         assistance availability.

IDENTIFY AREAS AT HIGHER RISK OF DISPLACEMENT

RESOURCES REVIEWED

Displacement Risk Map
The Washington State Department of Commerce developed a displacement risk map. 63
Displacement risk is assessed at the neighborhood level. A household is considered displaced if its
place of residence is disrupted due to forces outside of its control and it is unable to find suitable
replacement housing in the neighborhood. Displacement risk occurs when households are
experiencing greater pressure to leave and therefore, displacement risk analysis should inform
land use policymaking to encourage redevelopment and reinvestment in existing neighborhoods
while ensuring that existing neighborhood residents share in the benefits of that redevelopment
and reinvestment are not pushed out. The specific methodology used in the Commerce
displacement risk analysis is included in the state’s documentation.63

Figure 35 of the Comprehensive Plan includes a copy of the displacement risk map published by
Commerce.

     o   For unincorporated Clark County, the census tracts with a high risk for displacement are
         located in the unincorporated Vancouver Urban Growth Area along I-5 and Highway 99
         (West and Northeast Hazel Dell, northeast Felida, and Sherwood neighborhoods),
         Minnehaha area (Truman neighborhood) and Five Corners/Orchards area.
     o   For unincorporated Clark County, the census tracts identified as areas experiencing
         demographic and market change are located along the I-5 Corridor along Salmon Creek,
         on the outer edge of the Vancouver, Ridgefield, La Center urban growth areas and the
         rural areas in that vicinity.

Manufacture d Home Parks
     o   Unincorporated Clark County has 34 manufactured home parks (MHPs) that are home to
         just over 2,000 households in both urban growth areas and rural areas.
     o   A significant majority of MHPs are located inside unincorporated urban growth areas,
         primarily the Vancouver UGA.
     o   Many of the MHPs are located on parcels that are eligible for redevelopment at higher
         intensity for market-rate housing that could be more profitable for property owners,
         leading to park sales, rent increases, and park closures in some cases.
     o   Aging parks may also be facing costly infrastructure upgrade costs that push owners to sell
         and/or increase rents.

   o    MHP residents are uniquely vulnerable to displacement because they own their homes,
        they rent the space where their homes are sited; and there are often few alternatives
        when space rents are increased or parks are closed because manufactured homes are
        difficult or prohibitive to relocate, and there are few available spaces to move them.
   o    State regulations aim to cap rent increase to reduce displacement pressures, to lessen

   o    Clark County imposed a moratorium in August 2025, renewed through February 2027, to

   o    MHP study, preservation and support is also an adopted strategy in the County’s Housing

   o    Recent community feedback from MHP residents has generally aligned with the above
        information.

   •    The unincorporated Vancouver Urban Growth Area along I-5 and Highway 99 (West and
        Northeast Hazel Dell, northeast Felida, and Sherwood neighborhoods), Minnehaha area
        (Truman neighborhood) and Five Corners/Orchards area include census tracts with high

   •    Areas to monitor for demographic and market changes are located along the I-5 Corridor
        along Salmon Creek, the outer edges of the Vancouver, Ridgefield, and La Center urban

EXISTING GOAL, POLICY, STRATEGY AND CODE
AUDIT

AUDIT FRAMEWORK
The following overarching questions guided Clark County’s evaluation approach:

    •   Does this goal/policy/strategy/regulation contribute to racially disparate impacts or
        exclusion in housing?
    •   Is the goal/policy/strategy/regulation effective in accommodating more housing?
    •   Does the goal/policy/strategy/regulation increase displacement risk?


405                                                                                  A PPENDIX M
                                         CLARK2045
    •   Does the goal/policy/strategy/regulation provide protection to communities of interest
        from displacement?
    •   Does the goal/policy/strategy/regulation language include vague terms that could be used
        to marginalize communities of color?

Housing element goals, policies, strategies, and development regulations were reviewed through
the following lenses (modeled off of work conducted by the City of Bellevue and City of
Vancouver):

    1. Language clarity and potential for bias. Consider whether the policy includes use of coded
       or unclear language that can lead to inequitable application.
    2. Deficit-based language. Consider whether the policy uses language that can lead to an
       under-appreciation of the needs and contributions of people in specific groups.
    3. Impact on housing stock. Consider whether the policy introduces barriers, such as
       excessive regulation, or incentives to overall housing stock and affordable housing to meet
       the county’s goals.
    4. Impact on housing mix. Consider whether the policy prioritizes certain residential uses,
       and which uses are prioritized.
    5. Distribution of impact by geography, income, and community. Consider whether the
       policy creates benefits and burdens or risks that will be unevenly distributed.
    6. Mitigation for anticipated impacts. Consider whether the policy includes consideration of
       impacts and plans to mitigate them, including displacement risk.

Housing element goals, policies, strategies, and associated development regulations were
subsequently evaluated based on the following rubric provided in the Commerce guidance:

Table M.4. Existing housing element goal/policy/strategy/regulation evaluation framework
 Criteria                                                              Evaluation
 The goal/policy/strategy/regulation is valid and supports             S - Supportive
 meeting the identified housing needs. The policy is needed and
 addresses identified racially disparate impacts, displacement and
 exclusion in housing.
 The goal/policy/strategy/regulation can support meeting the           A - Approaching

 address racially disparate impacts, displacement and exclusion in
 housing.
 The goal/policy/strategy/regulation may challenge the                 C - Challenging

 policy’s benefits and burdens should be reviewed to optimize the
 ability to meet the policy’s objectives while improving the
 equitable distribution of benefits and burdens imposed by the

 The goal/policy/strategy/regulation does not impact the               NA - Not applicable

 displacement or exclusion.

A PPENDIX M                                                                                  406
                                           CLARK2045

After completing the goal, policy, strategy, and code audit and revisions, the code was reviewed
for consistency with Growth Management Act (GMA) goals, proposed countywide planning
policies and 20-year county planning policies.

Evaluation tools such as these are blunt and broad instruments and their impacts, intended and
unintended, unfold over the years. In the audit completed, goals/policies/strategies/development
regulations are assessed as being supportive, approaching, or challenging. This assessment is
useful but a highly simplified way of summarizing complex issues. Continued monitoring of
housing outcomes, community engagement, and continued policy, strategy, and regulation
refinement will be essential for the county to achieve its goals.

CONSISTENCY REVIEW
Housing element goals, policies, strategies, and associated development code were reviewed for
consistency with GMA goals, countywide planning policies and 20-year county policies. The
following list summarizes potential concerns.

   •   Exclusive language is found throughout Title 40 Development Code as noted above.
   •   Exclusive language is found in the background text of the Housing Element and in other
       Elements of the Comprehensive Plan.



423                                                                                      A PPENDIX M
                                          CLARK2045
    •   The term “character” is used in the GMA in unclear and possibly exclusive ways, including
        in RCW 36.70A.070(2) when describing the Housing Element, making it challenging for
        local jurisdictions to fully address terms like this when citing statute. Similarly, the term
        “citizen” is used in RCW 36.70A.020 in the GMA planning goal for public participation.
    •   The Land Use Element Countywide Planning Policies and Community Framework Plan
        policies reference previous housing density numbers and would need revisions to be
        consistent with the new requirements for planning for all economic segments of the
        population through the new housing by income band approach.
    •   Other Elements of the Comprehensive Plan would be more consistent with the Housing
        Element if they included policy language that better supported the Housing Element to
        begin to undo racially disparate impacts, included anti-displacement provisions, and used
        inclusive language.

APPENDIX N
Land Capacity Analysis

BACKGROUND

V A C A N T B U I L D A B L E L A N D S M O D E L ( VBL M)
The Vacant Buildable Lands Model (VBLM) is a planning tool developed to analyze residential,
commercial, and industrial lands within urban growth areas. The model serves as a tool for
evaluating urban area alternatives during Comprehensive Growth Management Plan updates and
for monitoring growth patterns during interim periods. The VBLM analyzes potential residential
and employment capacity of each urban growth area based on vacant and underutilized land
classifications. This potential capacity is used to determine the amount of urban land needed to
accommodate projected population and job growth for the next 20 years during plan updates and
to analyze land consumption or conversion rates on an annual basis for plan monitoring purposes.

The Vacant Buildable Lands Model has been rebuilt to run based on zoning instead of
comprehensive plan designation, as is required by HB1220 and included in guidance from the
Department of Commerce. The zoning-based model also allows for full implementation of changes
that were included in the 2021 Buildable Lands Report, to better capture residential development
on non-residential land. The achieved density numbers in the 2021 BLR were not able to be used
since the numbers were not reported based on zoning. Jurisdictions provided density estimates
for each zone and percentage splits, if a zone allows for both housing units and employment
capacity.

In general, the zoning-based model did not have a significant impact in capacity for the smaller
jurisdictions. The most significant increase in capacity was in the Vancouver UGA due to an
increase in zoning density anticipated as part of the proposed changes in the low density (single
family) residential zones within the unincorporated portion of the Vancouver UGA. The changes in
density reflect the increased density in the base zone, the allowance of duplexes, triplexes and
fourplexes, cottage housing, compact lot subdivisions, two ADU’s per lot and townhouse lots much
smaller than the base zone. This increase in capacity is consistent with the guidance from
Department of Commerce. However, this will require additional monitoring as part of the next
buildable lands report.

As part of the update process GIS staff created a process to document overrides to the model from
the local jurisdictions. The VBLM excludes publicly owned land, except Port Property, as not being
available for residential or employment capacity.




427                                                                                 A PPENDIX N
                                        CLARK2045
METHODOLOGY
The model classifies lands into three urban land use categories--residential, commercial, and
industrial. Lands are grouped into VBLM land use codes based on zoning designations for model
purposes. Lands designated as parks & open space, public facility, mining lands, or airport within
the urban growth areas are excluded from available land calculations. Additionally, all rural and
urban reserve designated lands are excluded from the model.

The model classifies each urban parcel by its utilization as built, vacant, or underutilized by the
three major land uses. Additionally lands with potential environmental concerns and/or geologic
hazards as consistent with the applicable section of the Clark County and other municipal codes
are classified as constrained (critical lands) lands. Constrained lands are identified by parcel in the
model. Constrained lands include:

    •   100 year floodplain or flood fringe
    •   Wetlands inventory (NWI, high quality, permitted, modeled) with 100 foot buffer
    •   Slopes greater than 15 percent (>25% for City of Vancouver)
    •   Land slide area that has active or historically unstable slopes
    •   Designated shorelines
    •   Hydric soils with 50 foot buffer
    •   Habitat areas with 100 foot buffer Species areas with 300 foot buffer
    •   Riparian stream buffers by stream type

The VBLM classifies all of the land inside the UGA based on the criteria described below. Parcels
of land classified as Vacant, Underutilized, Redevelopable, or Vacant Platted Lots are the vacant
buildable lands used to calculate the capacity of these lands in terms of population and jobs.

RESIDENTIAL MODEL
Important residential classifications include vacant, vacant critical, underutilized, and
underutilized critical. These classes are used to determine gross acres available for development.
Vacant exempt, vacant lots less than 5,000 square feet and all other classes are excluded from
available land calculations.

Criteria for classifying residential lands are as follows:

    •   Residential Vacant Criteria
        o Building value indexed based on building value trend
        o Not tax exempt
        o Not an easement or right of way
        o Not a state assessed or institutional parcel
        o Not a mobile home park
        o Not an excluded Property Type (Golf Courses, Stables, Driving Ranges, Assisted Living
           Facilities) Parcel greater than 5,000 square feet
        o Vacant Platted Lots

       o   Lot platted within last 20 years
       o   Minimum parcel size 1,000 sq. ft.
       o   Maximum parcel size of 1 acre
   •   Underutilized
       o Same as Vacant except building value criteria is replaced with a building value per acre
          criteria.
       o Building value per acre of land is below the 10th percentile of building value per acre
          for all residential parcels within all UGAs. The 10th percentile is calculated by the

   •   Constrained (Critical lands)

          lands are described above.

COMMERCIAL AND INDUSTRIAL MODELS
Commercial and industrial lands are classified using consistent criteria.

Important commercial classes for determining gross acres available for development include
vacant, vacant critical, underutilized, and underutilized critical. Vacant exempt and vacant lots less
than 4,000 square feet are excluded from available land calculations.

Important industrial classes for determining gross acres available for development include vacant,
vacant critical, exempt vacant port property, exempt vacant port property critical, underutilized,
underutilized critical, exempt underutilized port property, and exempt underutilized port
property critical. All exempt not port properties are excluded in the available land calculations.

Commercial and industrial models classify vacant and underutilized land as follows:

   •   Vacant land
       o Building value indexed based on trends in property value.
       o Commercial and Industrial Sites are often composed of multiple parcels.
       o Parcels that grouped into a site by the Assessor are classified as built regardless of the
          building value or building value per acre criteria.
       o Not Exempt.
           Port property is Tax exempt, but is still eligible to be classified as vacant or
              underutilized.
       o Not an Easement or right of way
       o Parcel greater than 4,000 square feet
       o Not a state assessed or institutional parcel


429                                                                                    A PPENDIX N
                                      CLARK2045
   •   Underutilized Lands
       o Same as vacant except building value criteria is replaced with a building value per acre
          criteria.
   •   Vacant commercial and industrial properties with active businesses are reclassified as
       underutilized
   •   Constrained (Critical lands)
       o All classifications may be subdivided into constrained vs. not constrained. Commercial
          and industrial constrained lands are defined the same as residential constrained lands
          and are listed above.
   •   Port Properties in the Commercial and Industrial Model
       o Port owned properties are not excluded from the model base on their tax exempt
          status. Buildable port properties are included in available land calculations.
       o Port properties can be classified as vacant, underutilized, or constrained.


PLANNING ASSUMPTIONS
The next step in the buildable lands process is to calculate the yield. This is done by applying
planning assumptions to the vacant buildable lands. These assumptions account for infrastructure,
reduced development on constrained land, and market factors. These assumptions are used to
deduct acreage from the gross vacant buildable land. The yield is based on the acres of net vacant
multiplied by the assumed number of houses or jobs per acre of net vacant land.

Residential Model Planning Assumptions:

   •   31.5% deduction to account for on-site infrastructure needs. 20% infrastructure
       deduction for mixed use lands.
   •   Never to convert factor
       o 10% for vacant land
       o 30% for underutilized
   •   50% of available constrained (critical) land will not convert
   •   Mixed Use VBLM land uses have a percentage of their net vacant land allocated to
       housing, and the remainder to jobs
   •   Redevelopment
       o New classification for small underutilized lots in Urban High Density (0.5-1ac, no more
          than one housing unit, assuming 10% redevelopment)
       o New classification for small underutilized lots in Urban Low Density (0.5-1ac, no more
          than one housing unit, assuming 5% redevelopment)
   •   50% of Vancouver Urban High will develop as plats
   •   50% of Vancouver Urban High will develop as sites with no infrastructure deduction

Commercial and Industrial Model Planning Assumptions

   •   25% infrastructure factor applied for both commercial and industrial lands.

A PPENDIX N                                                                                     430
                                        CLARK2045
     •   20% of available constrained (critical) commercial and mixed use land will not convert
     •   50% of available constrained (critical) industrial land will not convert
     •   40% of mixed use land will develop as commercial, 15% commercial for Battle Ground
         mixed use - residential and 75% commercial for mixed use - employment.
     •   5% residential redevelopment rate on built Vancouver City Center commercial;
     •   1% residential redevelopment rate on Vancouver built commercial outside City Center
     •   30% of commercial land in the Vancouver City Center will be residential development and
         15% of Vancouver commercial land outside the City Center will be residential
         development

Employees and unit per acre density assumptions are applied to net developable acres to predict
future employment and housing unit capacities. Densities are set based on achieved density
figures by each jurisdiction by VBLM Land Use Type 64. Applied residential densities vary by UGA.

Applied employment densities vary by land use as well. Commercial classes which include
commercial, business park, and mixed use categories apply 20 employees per acre while industrial
classes apply 9 employees per acre.

Applying residential and employment planning assumptions to the VBLM results produce housing
units and employment carrying capacity estimates for urban growth areas. These estimates help
monitor growth on an annual basis and is part of the criteria used for setting UGA boundaries
during growth management plan updates.

Underutilized land classes are grouped with vacant classes by land use in Maps Online and on
other map products.

APPENDIX O
Housing Barriers & Strategies Matrix

Clark County’s 2022 Housing Options Study and Action Plan (HOSAP) committed the County to a
range of housing actions that address identified barriers to housing production within the County.
Items in the table identified with an asterisk (*) indicate a potential high impact. Additional details
are included as follows:

    •   The County adopted development regulations in 2024 that address a first phase (Phase 1)
        of those actions, and is proposing adoption of a second phase (Phase 2) of those actions in
        tandem with the 2025 Comprehensive Plan adoption.
    •   Additional HOSAP strategies beyond Phase 1 and 2 include actions grouped around
        Housing Options, Affordable Housing, Programs and Partnerships, and Advocacy,
        intended for future phases of implementation (Future).
    •   Additional actions beyond the HOSAP strategies are also proposed with the 2025
        Comprehensive Plan implementation (CPI), as included in the following table.
    •   Where relevant, actions are noted as affecting the low-density residential zones (R1
        zones) or the medium- and high-density residential zones (R zones).
